CHAIR ( Senator Green ): I now declare open this hearing of the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee for the budget estimates 2025-26. The Senate has referred to the committee the particulars of proposed expenditure for 2025-26 for the portfolios of Home Affairs and Attorney-General's and other related documents. These are budget estimates proceedings, and the outcomes to be heard in today's estimates are from the Home Affairs and Attorney-General's portfolios. The committee has set Thursday 29 May as the date by which answers to questions on notice are to be returned. The committee has also decided that written questions on notice should be provided to the secretariat by 5 pm on Wednesday 16 April, 2025.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence to the committee. Officers and senators are familiar with the rules of the Senate governing estimates hearings. If you need assistance, the secretariat has copies of the rules.

The Senate, by resolution in 1999, endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has also resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution prohibits only questions asking for opinions on matters of policy, and this does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. I particularly draw the attention of witnesses to an order of the Senate of 13 May 2009 specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, which will be incorporated into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

CHAIR: Witnesses are specifically reminded that a statement that information or a document is confidential or consists of advice to government is not a statement that meets the requirements of the 2009 order. Instead, witnesses are required to provide some specific indication of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or the document.

I remind senators of their obligation under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect.

Department of Home Affairs

[09:03]

CHAIR: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Murray Watt representing the Minister for Home Affairs. I also call officers from the Department of Home Affairs in relation to cross-portfolio, corporate and general matters. Minister, would you like to make an opening statement?

Senator Watt: No, thank you, Chair. Great to see you all again. I'm sure I speak for everyone behind me.

CHAIR: Ms Foster, would you like to make an opening statement before we go to questions?

Ms Foster : No, thank you.

CHAIR: Thank you. I will hand the call to Senator Paterson to kick us off.

Senator PATERSON: It's good to see you again, Ms Foster and officials. I'm grateful for your assistance, as always. Secretary, I wrote to you about a week ago in relation to questions on notice that were outstanding. What, if any, action have you taken since that letter to address outstanding questions on notice?

Ms Foster : I spoke with the area that coordinates the questions for us to ask them for an update on where we're at, what we had to do. I then spoke to my leadership team and emphasised that this was an extraordinary priority for me, to have them personally focus on getting as many done as possible. I felt the benefit of that by the flow that came through to me personally for clearance over the course of this week. So we've had a real push—I mean, we were pressing, but we've had an additional push—since we got your letter. We have managed to finalise a large number since then, but whether or not we have given the minister's office enough time to then have them lodged is another question. But we have pulled out all stops to try and get them answered.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. I am grateful for that. As you say, it may well be the case that you've cleared a lot from your end but we haven't necessarily seen it at our end. Obviously, there's a step in the process between you clearing them and us receiving them, which is the minister's office, as you say. Does the department track performance against questions on notice being answered on time? Have you got a good sense of what has and hasn't been answered and whether timelines have been met?

Ms Foster : We do. I don't know the details, and either Ms Sharpe or Mr Hickey could help me with how we do that. Whether or not we keep a running metric, I don't know. What I do know is that we have been very conscious that we have had a number of outstanding ones from previous hearings that we have been trying hard to clear so that we can maintain a record of doing them on time.

Senator PATERSON: Do you know how many are outstanding as of today?

Ms Foster : I'm sure Ms Sharpe or Mr Hickey will be able to help you with the exact number. It's been changing a lot this week.

Ms Sharpe: The question was how many are outstanding as of today from the most recent estimates?

Senator PATERSON: All estimates.

Ms Sharpe: From the most recent February estimates period, of the 493 questions we took on notice, 153 have been tabled with the committee, leaving 340 outstanding. From the November 2024 estimates hearings, of the 676 that we took on notice, 539 have been tabled, leaving 139 outstanding. From the May 2024 budget estimates, of the 1,000 that we took on notice, 946 have been tabled, leaving 54 outstanding.

Senator PATERSON: For the May and November estimates hearings, has the department provided draft answers to the minister's office in all instances, or is the department still working through some of those 54 and 139 outstanding questions?

Ms Sharpe: We have provided drafts for the majority; I'd have to check whether it's all of them. They're with the minister's office. In some cases they have been returned for further work.

Senator PATERSON: Can you break down for me, please, the proportion of those 139 and 54, in the first instance, where the draft is with the minister's office and the proportion where they're with Home Affairs for further work.

Ms Sharpe: For the November hearings, as of yesterday, 132 are with the minister's office. For the May estimates hearings, 52 are with the minister's office.

Senator PATERSON: Do you know how long those have been with the minister's office?

Ms Sharpe: I don't have that detail with me. I'd have to check, because that's a large number and I'd have to go through each one.

Senator PATERSON: Obviously, the overwhelming majority of those questions are with the minister's office, not the department. What can you tell me about the questions that are with the department for further work?

Ms Sharpe: I'd have to take that detail on notice as well. I don't have the detail of the content of those.

Senator PATERSON: I enjoy the irony of taking questions on notice about questions on notice, as I'm sure you do too. Of the more recent round of estimates, the 340 that are outstanding, how many have been provided to the minister's office?

Ms Sharpe: As at yesterday, there were 312 with the minister's office.

Senator PATERSON: To be fair, my observation on that is that the department appears to have done its job in providing draft responses to questions. I don't know when exactly they were provided to the minister's office—perhaps it was quite recently—but it looks like the department is largely holding up its end of the bargain. The backlog appears to be with the minister's office. Is that a fair observation?

Ms Foster : I just make the observation I did earlier: that there's been a very tight turnaround on this most recent estimates.

Senator PATERSON: Yes.

Ms Foster : So many of those answers have gone up in the very recent past.

Senator PATERSON: Yes, I appreciate that, and I do understand that in relation to the most recent round of estimates, but it's a harder argument to sustain for the November round, let alone the May round of estimates.

I'd like to follow up some specific outstanding questions on notice that are in my name. For example, from the May round—as of yesterday, at least—BE24-0064 is outstanding. It was a question about the number of AAT set-aside decisions that the government appealed to the Federal Court since direction 99 took effect. That was taken on notice. I presume that's one of the answers that the department has prepared an answer for but on which it's waiting for ministerial clearance.

Ms Sharpe: We'll just check while we're here so we can confirm the status of that one exactly.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. Is it possible the department could provide that response before outcome 2 today, because I have follow-up questions that will depend on what the answer to that question is?

Ms Sharpe: We'll see what we can do, yes.

Senator PATERSON: It is almost a year ago now that that question was asked, and, as you know, the timeliness expected by the Senate is much more than that. Another question on direction 99 was BE24-0052. It was asking about whether direction 99 had come about at the instruction of the minister or whether it was a recommendation from the department. I was told that it was an iterative process. Is there any more detail on this iterative process?

Ms Sharpe: I'd have to check the specifics of that one.

Senator PATERSON: Okay. I'd be grateful if an answer could be provided in advance of outcome 2 today. Another one, again from May last year, BE24-0102, was for a breakdown of the location of NZYQ-affected individuals by local government area. It was taken on notice by the ABF commissioner. What are my prospects of getting an answer to that before outcome 3 today?

Ms Sharpe: We will do what we can.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. Do you know if that's one of the ones that are sitting with the department or sitting with the minister's office?

Ms Sharpe: I'm just having my team check as we're talking. I've just got confirmation they're with the minister's office.

Senator PATERSON: Okay. Do you know when that one was provided to the minister's office?

Ms Sharpe: We'll see what we can get while we're here and get you that detail.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. That would be good. Another one from that round of estimates is BE24-0109. I asked how many of the then 26 sex offenders that were not subject to electronic monitoring were formerly child sex offenders. That was taken on notice. Obviously, there've been more sex offenders released since, but is the department able to answer that question today?

Ms Foster : We'll see what we can do.

Senator PATERSON: Okay. I've got a lot more to go through here. How about question on notice 45 from that round? It is NZYQ related again, from the spillover hearing that was held a little bit after. I asked for the details of the state and territory criminal offences committed by the cohort, including a breakdown of the types of offences, their location by state and territory, their custodial status and whether or not they were subject to electronic monitoring or curfews at the time of their offending. Has the department drafted a response to that question?

Ms Foster : Senator, I think, to save time, we will probably have to check each one, because we don't have the full list of them in front of us. So perhaps, if you give us those you're interested in, we can do that.

Senator PATERSON: Sure. This is why I wrote to you a week ago asking that this be prioritised, and your evidence is that you have prioritised it, and I'm grateful for that. But we do need the cooperation of the minister's office for Senate estimates to function, because these are legitimate questions in the public interest. Some of them go to public safety, and I don't think it is adequate to have them not answered for almost a year, particularly if they've been sitting with the minister's office for that length of that time or for most of that time.

The other one I have a question about is No. 47 from that round of estimates, which was about bridging visa holders who are not living in a situation that poses a risk to the welfare of others. Question 22 from the November round was about why the Minister for Home Affairs was not present at the ASIO announcement on the raising of the terrorist threat level. Do we have any update on that?

Ms Foster : I think that was one that the minister took on notice.

Senator PATERSON: I think you might be right, and it's a straightforward question. Was the minister invited? Why was he not invited? Was he invited but he couldn't attend? Minister, do you have an update on that?

Senator Watt: I don't, but I'll check the status of that one.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you; I appreciate that. No. 23 from that round of estimates was about advice to the minister about his electric vehicle. That hasn't been answered. Minister, could you follow up with the minister's office on that one today please?

Senator Watt: Sure.

Senator PATERSON: No. 56 from the November estimates round was about whether the humanitarian places for Palestinian visa holders were going to be in the 20,000 places allocated by the government to the humanitarian program or on top of the 20,000 places. Do we have an answer to that?

Ms Foster : We'll follow that up.

Senator PATERSON: Do you know, though, Ms Foster, whether or not those—

Ms Foster : That's why I'm frowning. I think that—I'm not sure. Let me have the answer checked.

Senator PATERSON: That would be helpful if you could. That's an outcome 2 matter that I'd like to pursue. Chair, I'm about to move on to another topic, so I just want to check whether you want to rotate the call or whether I can keep it?

CHAIR: You can keep the call. I will hand it over in about 10 minutes.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you; I appreciate that. I want to move to some budget matters, particularly the department's budget allocation in the most recent budget this week. On page 14 of the portfolio budget statement, what does it show about the Department of Home Affairs' total funding from this financial year to the next financial year?

Ms Foster : I'll get our chief operating officer, Ms Tressler, to take you through that.

Ms Tressler : I will actually get assistance on this particular question from our chief financial officer.

Mr Harvey : It's a broad question, but essentially it shows, under 'Departmental' and 'Administered', that we've largely got similar levels of funding in 2024-25 and 2025-26.

Senator PATERSON: Unless I'm reading this wrong, your definition and my definition of 'similar' are a bit different. Can you read to me the total resourcing for Home Affairs in the 2024-25 financial year.

Mr Harvey : I can. At the bottom, it goes from $9.1 billion down to $8.57 billion. A lot of that is due to just—

Senator PATERSON: Before we go to the explanation—is my maths right that that's about a $600 million reduction in one financial year?

Mr Harvey : With those numbers, yes. But if I could explain—

Senator PATERSON: I will come to that. I will give you the opportunity to explain it; don't worry. I want to dig into it in detail. Do you really think a $600 million reduction year on year is a similar amount of funding? It seems like quite a big reduction in funding.

Mr Harvey : The reason I said that is that there's money provided this year, there was money provided to us last year and then there's money carried over from prior years. That prior-year funding is money that is sitting there at the top of each of those sections. That money available is just dropped during the year, but it doesn't go to the level of funding we're provided to run the department this year. Prior-year appropriations can lapse after a few years. They just drop away through normal housekeeping—

Senator PATERSON: Sure, but it means that the department has fewer resources at its disposal, doesn't it?

Mr Harvey : Less cash available. But we have budget—if I could turn to a different page, it might help to show it a bit better.

Senator PATERSON: Please; go ahead.

Mr Harvey : The profit and loss of the department is on page 65—the income statement. The total expense line there has gone from $4.109 million in 2024-25 to $4.111 million, which is roughly the same level of funding provided to the department.

Senator PATERSON: What does it show for the next financial year after that?

Mr Harvey : In 2026-27, it drops, as you were pointing out there, to $3.5 million.

Senator PATERSON: How much of a reduction is that?

Mr Harvey : About $600 million.

Senator PATERSON: That seems, to me, like a big reduction in one financial year.

Ms Tressler : This is not an unusual profile for the department's funding. There are a range of particular items that we have been funded for many years on an annual basis. One of those, as an example, is OSB, and Mr Harvey can take you through more detail on that. We also have other particular types of funding which are very much based on variable funding. Each year we do estimates based on activity to estimate funding. So we do typically see that there are adjustments within the year made up as estimates variations that do increase our funding over time, and, as Mr Harvey has been saying, our departmental appropriation and administered appropriation between this year and next financial year is staying relatively stable, and we're confident that, if there's a requirement to vary our funding, then that case would be put forward in accordance with our normal practices.

Senator PATERSON: Yes. Mr Pezzullo and I had lengthy discussion about this in a previous round of Senate estimates. Are you telling me: 'Let's rely on these figures on page 65,' and that the drop between 2025-26 and 2026-27 won't eventuate and that, in reality, there won't be a $600 million cut to the department's resources?

Ms Foster : That would not be consistent with previous experience. Previous experience would indicate that that will level out with annual funding and additional measures.

Senator PATERSON: How confident are you that that cut of $600 million won't eventuate?

Ms Foster : Senator, I can't predict what decisions government will make in the future. All I can do—

Senator PATERSON: Sure, but you're trying to reassure me that I shouldn't worry about it. So why shouldn't I?

Ms Foster : Because our historical funding would indicate that that is an unlikely outcome.

Senator PATERSON: So, based on your experience, you're confident that that $600 million cut won't eventuate and will be topped up in a subsequent budget?

Ms Tressler : If I could, I will provide some examples. There's the OSB one that I mentioned. In this particular budget, the department receives $267 million for our Operation Sovereign Borders. That was for one year. That's been the case for many years. Another is our offshore funding for Nauru. We are provided with the funding that we require over the next year and also to keep the facility in hot contingency. If we find that we've got the numbers that are still on Nauru, then we process an estimates variation, and that funding will increase accordingly. On our visa variable funding side, if the volumes are such that we require additional funding, then that's provided through an estimates variation as well. So we do get big chunks of funding—

Senator PATERSON: Yes, I do appreciate that. So what would the consequences be for the department if government didn't make a decision to add that additional funding in that financial year?

Senator Watt: Noting that that would not be the practice that has been adopted.

Ms Foster : It would depend on what was not funded.

Senator PATERSON: Ms Tressler gave a couple of examples. One of them was OSB. If the government didn't make a decision to top up the funding of OSB in a subsequent budget, what would that mean for Operation Sovereign Borders?

Ms Foster : I'm hesitating just because that is speculative, particularly when we have not seen that outcome previously.

Senator PATERSON: It's not that speculative though, because it's printed in black and white in the budget papers. This is what they say: there will be a fall in funding of $600 million between those two financial years unless, as you say, the government makes a decision, which you can't guarantee, to increase that funding in that financial year.

Ms Foster : But, as I've said, our experience is that that is done. I don't find it feasible that that would not happen.

Senator PATERSON: Minister, can you give a guarantee that the government will top up that funding in that financial year to ensure there's not a cut to Operation Sovereign Borders and other important programs?

Senator Watt: What I'm hearing is that it's been the consistent practice of governments to top up that funding, and I've got no reason to think that that wouldn't occur if and when we are re-elected.

Senator PATERSON: So we should add $600 million to the deficit for that financial year on Mr Chalmers's budget?

Senator Watt: I know that your leader is now proposing to increase taxes on Australians in the next term by repealing tax cuts.

Senator PATERSON: This is a question about your budget handed down two days ago. Are you guaranteeing there will be a $600 million top-up, and, therefore, should we add $600 million to Mr Chalmers's deficit?

Senator Watt: I've already answered the question in terms of what the government's intentions would be.

Senator PATERSON: You can't have it both ways. You can't say, 'Don't worry, we won't allow funding to fall,' but also, 'Don't worry, we won't increase the deficit by $600 million.' It's one or the other—or are you going to find other offsetting savings for that $600 million you have to find? Are you going to increase taxes by $600 million to offset that?

Senator Watt: I'm informed by the department—and I'm sure they're happy to elaborate—that the practice that we've been discussing is one that has happened under governments of Labor persuasions and governments of coalition persuasions. I admire your attempt to concoct something here, but you're concocting something that happened under the last coalition government as well.

Senator PATERSON: This is your budget, Minister. This is—

Senator Watt: It's a very good budget, I think.

Senator PATERSON: in black and white. This is printed in the budget papers. There will be a $600 million cut to the department, including to Operation Sovereign Borders, unless the government adds funding. So either reassure the Australian people that you are not going to cut Operation Sovereign Borders or come clean to the Australian people that Mr Chalmers's deficits for that year will be $600 million higher because you haven't provisioned for this.

Senator Watt: I think that the Australian people can look at what this government has done in relation to Operation Sovereign Borders, which is to have provided $1.8 billion more funding than the former coalition government projected. So I think the Australian people can feel very confident about the level of funding that will be provided by the Albanese government to Operation Sovereign Borders.

Senator PATERSON: How's that working out in terms of surveillance hours and maritime patrol days and boats—

Senator Watt: You'll have all the time in the world to ask about—

Senator PATERSON: slipping through and reaching the Australian mainland?

Senator Watt: You'll have all the time to ask the personnel from Operation Sovereign Borders later in the program, but my recollection of their previous evidence is that they've been very satisfied with the amount of resourcing that they've been provided with—

Senator PATERSON: I'm not sure the Australian people will agree that more than 25 boats in two years—

Senator Watt: We can talk about the boats that got here when Peter Dutton was the Home Affairs minister—

Senator PATERSON: including seven reaching the Australian mainland or a territory is a good result.

Senator Watt: and we can go round and round in circles.

CHAIR: Senator Ghosh.

Senator GHOSH: I'd like to thank the officials for being here today and for all the work that goes into preparing for these sessions, particularly on very short notice on this occasion. Senator GHOSH: My questions relate to cybersecurity and the government's cyber strategy.

Ms Foster : Some combination of Mr Hansford and Mr Chapman will be able to help you with that.

Senator GHOSH: Wonderful. I understand that we've recently had the publication of the Cyber Security Act's Cyber Incident Review Board rules, the Cyber Security Act ransomware rules and smart device rules as well. We've had a series of rules published in the recent past. Are you able to give us a quick summary about what each of those do, and I do mean quite quickly or just at a high level, please.

Mr Hansford : Certainly. You might recall that, following the passage of the Cyber Security Act last year, we did consult from December out to February on a series of different rules. Mr Bell has been leading those consultations, so I might get him to outline each of the different four measures in detail.

Mr Bell : To your question, and keeping it short, the three sets of rules that were consulted on reflected three of the measures from the Cyber Security Act. The first was around security standards for smart devices. The second was ransomware payment reporting. And the third was the Cyber Incident Review Board.

Taking those from the top, the first one was around the security standards for smart devices. These were the rules that would set the first standard under the legislation, and this would be for mandating security standards for smart devices. The rules set out the standards but also cover off some of the administrative elements.

The second one that was covered is the ransomware payment reporting. That was about the obligation for reporting business entities to provide a ransomware payment report to the Australian Signals Directorate and the Department of Home Affairs upon payment of a ransom. In the rules, the focus for those provisions was around setting the annual turnover threshold for the reporting obligation as well as, again, some other administrative matters.

The third one was around the Cyber Incident Review Board. These were a lot of the governance rules around establishing the Cyber Incident Review Board, which would establish an advisory body to conduct no-fault post-incident reviews of significant cybersecurity incidents and make recommendations to prevent, detect, respond to and minimise the impact of cyber incidents in the future. So, the governance parameters were the focus as well as other rules around eligibility criteria.

Mr Hansford : It's been a bit of a long and winding road on the reform. For people watching, 30 May is the time for ransomware reporting. That's the next big thing that businesses with a revenue threshold over $3 million should expect—that is, to report ransomware payments from 30 May. And then people who are developing products for the Australian economy, Internet of Things product, are really thinking about how they might meet the deadline of March 2026 to start to meet those three obligations that are imposed on them. I think they're the two big takeaways.

Senator GHOSH: Thank you. In terms of the number of people within the department who work on the Cyber Security Strategy and its various manifestations, are you able to give me an estimate of the FTE who are dedicated to that?

Mr Hansford : I certainly am. It's slightly tricky in the sense that the cybersecurity strategy—to the evidence earlier today—funded the critical infrastructure function in the package of $586.9 million that was announced at the same time as the strategy back in November 2023. That is funding for almost a hundred people devoted to that function.

Equally, though, there are a range of different measures that have been funded in the strategy. Mr Bell manages a lot of those. Mr Neal also manages the government security uplift element and has a component of about 40 people that was funded in the context of the cybersecurity strategy. Directly on the cybersecurity strategy itself, in addition to other individuals who might work on regulatory cyber issues—having the transport security legislation passed last night, for example—there are a range of people who take cybersecurity as part of their role. And then, Mr Anstee and Mr Bell, in your particular areas you have people directly supporting the implementation of the cyber strategy.

Mr Anstee : I might add those specific numbers, if they're of interest. Under Horizon 1, the allocated FTE was 57.5 ASL. For the broader strategy package to continue the security of critical infrastructure measures that Mr Hansford mentioned, there are 102 ASL.

Senator GHOSH: In terms of the Cyber and Infrastructure Security Centre group, are you able to tell me by what amount the headcount or FTE has increased since July 2022 or thereabouts?

Mr Hansford : Since July 2022, the structures have slightly changed. I might take it from May 2023, which is when the group came together in its current form. It's fair to say that, right now, the funding is for about 480 people, and that is an increase from the year prior. The figures that you've heard, particularly in relation to the funding of the critical infrastructure function as well as the cybersecurity strategy, are an increase to the number of staff in the group, along with the government cybersecurity function. That was all funded in the cybersecurity strategy. That's been the biggest funding increase and added additional FTE to the group. In August of 2023 we had the Protective Security Policy Framework come into the group, and staff have been transferred from the Attorney-General's Department. We've also had a few functions transferred from the Digital Transformation Agency—all of which have increased the number to 480-odd. So it is an increase from where we started in May 2023. But, equally, if you look back to July of 2022, there has been an increase.

Senator GHOSH: Thank you for the detail in that answer. What current priorities are in the lowest one-fifth or 20 per cent in terms of what the department's working on?

Mr Hansford : I'd say in response to that question that everything that everyone in my group undertakes is a priority. We have a very important mission. We take our job very, very seriously. With the available resources, we look at the program of work that we can undertake. Just to take an example, we have a whole team devoted to transport security compliance. We have field officers, transport security inspectors, who are on the ground at airports every day of the week, looking at compliance issues. If we had more, we'd do more work. If we had less, we'd do less work; we'd reprioritise. So I wouldn't categorise the lowest one-fifth body of work. I think all of our work is very, very important. We allocate our resources to the areas of priority that we're focused on.

Senator GHOSH: Respectfully, everything can't be a priority. In terms of how you do prioritise, currently, what's at the top of your list and what's at the bottom of your list?

Mr Hansford : Well, at the very top of our list is the implementation of our legislative priorities that are legislatively mandated, particularly those that relate to timing of activity, if there's a particular legislative requirement. So that's very much at top of our list. But what governs our priorities is our key performance indicators in our corporate plan. They govern the day-to-day work. Effectively, when you dig down, they are developed on the material functions that the department undertakes.

Each of our KPIs in my group links to the priorities that we are focused on as a group. To amplify those priorities, at least for the last couple of years, in January I try to put a narrative for all my staff in the group around what our priorities are, where they link, in terms of KPIs, where they link to the Administrative Arrangements Order and how they link to some of the environmental issues that are happening across the world—for example, a persistent cybersecurity threat. Equally, we have a whole range of priorities on cybersecurity, a dynamic critical infrastructure security threat environment, and a very key focus on those outcomes. Overlaid on that is the funding that government gives us. That's how we, effectively, prioritise our work. You see the results of that work in our annual report every year and see glimpses of it in Senate estimates.

Senator GHOSH: Sure. Cybersecurity is obviously a global issue and is something that governments around the world are dealing with. Do you have any insight as to where Australia's cybersecurity strategy sits and our resourcing levels are relative to equivalent developed countries in the OECD—for instance, Canada, New Zealand or the United Kingdom?

Mr Hansford : Certainly. I'd describe us as being comparable with a range of like-minded jurisdictions. But when you look at different strategies across the world, lots of people take different approaches. The cybersecurity strategy in the United States—to take one example—is very conceptual, and we look to that, for example, in the development of our own cybersecurity strategy. Singapore has a very strong focus on government security, and we have very strong partnerships with it. We are actually assisting the government of New Zealand at the moment with their cybersecurity strategy to make sure that, between our two countries, there is a level of complementarity.

Our ambition in cybersecurity strategy is to be a global leader by 2030, and some of the elements that we are demonstrating, both in our strategy but I think also in our implementation, pick up on and reflect some of the same issues being considered by some of our partners. It's quite remarkable, when you look at the cybersecurity and critical infrastructure related work programs in a country like Japan, that a lot of the issues it is looking at are very similar to the issues that we are looking at—

Senator GHOSH: Sorry to cut you off, but are those other countries increasing, decreasing or maintaining their level of investment in cybersecurity, from a governmental perspective?

Mr Hansford : It all depends. Some countries are focused on different areas of cybersecurity. Our strategy for the first horizon—actually for the seven years but particularly for the range of funding initiatives in the first horizon—as I said, has $586.9 million. I've seen other countries invest in different areas of priority. We work with a range of different countries on a very frequent basis. Some fund them quite significantly; others take a conceptual approach. So it really does depend and vary. I'm not sure if Mr Bell would like to add to that.

Mr Bell : I think one of the key things that we've certainly heard in our feedback and bilateral engagement is about some of the novel regulatory approaches that Australia has been developing and undertaking. One of the examples from our Cyber Security Act last year was the 'limited use obligation'. That's one particular initiative that has gotten a lot of interest from international partners, because it's a challenge that a lot of jurisdictions face about how you ensure that you're managing the regulatory elements for cybersecurity but at the same time not chilling businesses' confidence in providing information. Another big piece of work that we're doing is looking at the efficacy of the strategy, so we've done a lot of evaluation and monitoring work. We have had a lot of interest from foreign counterparts about that work, which is quite novel and groundbreaking.

Ms Foster : I'm looking to the chair for guidance. We've covered the technology policy angles. This goes more to—

Mr Hansford : No. It's the same assessment that relates to foreign ownership control and influence in relation to the direction from July last year. Equally, though, the Protective Security Policy Framework applies to all vendors and all procurements by non-corporate Commonwealth entities.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Other platforms such as Signal, I think, are formally owned by Russian oligarchs who now reside somewhere in Dubai or the United Arab Emirates; is that right?

Senator PATERSON: I think that's Telegram.

Mr Hansford : Two points. The first one is we expect every non-corporate Commonwealth entity to undertake a stocktake of their existing technology. That's done at an individual agency level, including our own department. As the central policy function, we will expect to see the results of that analysis from every department in their reporting in the PSPF annual report. The second point is that where we see extreme risk we advise the secretary about the issuance of a direction. Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Does the July 2024 determination set out the process, including extreme risk?

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Mr Neal, you might help here. It's quite opaque from outsiders. There's the July directive to look at risk, including from foreign owned and controlled entities. Second, conduct a risk assessment of potential FOCI risks during the procurement of the technology assets and processes. Third, and most importantly, regularly monitor the entity's contracts relating to the technology assets to ensure that FOCI risks do not materialise in accordance with PSPF policy 6.

In addition to those three, we do provide a significant amount of ongoing guidance through the policy explanatory note and detailed engagements. We had about 2,500 engagements on the PSPF hotline last year, where we provided that direct advice to entities as they were procuring our access and technology.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Minister, we're quite imminently going into an election. There is a real risk that Elon Musk will use his platform to agitate for far-right politics in Australia in this election—an active risk of foreign interference. Don't you think that that should be under review?

Senator Watt: As I say, I think all attempts at foreign interference are things we need to take seriously, and we always need to ensure that our policy framework is current and strong to deal with those attempts. I'm sure the officials will give that consideration.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: They've haven't been.

CHAIR: Senator Paterson, you have the call again.

Senator PATERSON: I want to quickly follow up the line of questioning from Senator Shoebridge on one issue before moving on to another topic. Mr Hansford, I think I heard you say in response to Senator Shoebridge that the reason why the government had to take action under the PSPF on those specific apps is that they represented an 'extreme risk'. Did I hear you right?

Mr Hansford : Yes.

Senator PATERSON: Kaspersky and DeepSeek represented an extreme risk. I assume, flowing on from that, that you regard TikTok as an extreme risk as well.

Mr Hansford : Yes.

Senator PATERSON: Given that, has the government used the powers available to it under the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act to also require critical infrastructure operators to remove those pieces of software?

Mr Hansford : No, but when the secretary issued the direction, both on DeepSeek and on Kaspersky, we took a number of actions to write to all critical infrastructure in the country, outlining the risks and encouraging them to also take similar action. And we have had reports that a lot of critical infrastructure have taken the action, particularly as it relates to DeepSeek. We've also done that with state and territory governments.

Senator PATERSON: Did you do the same for TikTok?

Mr Hansford : It wasn't in the department at the time—

Senator PATERSON: That's fair.

Mr Hansford : but I do recall having discussions with infrastructure owners and operators back in 2023, yes.

Senator PATERSON: Do you think critical infrastructure owners would understand that TikTok represents an extreme cybersecurity risk?

Mr Hansford : I think, when you look at vendor risk, actually a lot of people don't understand particularly the foreign ownership, control and influence. And there is a role for the government, which is why this month we released a risk assessment guidance, which is available on our website, about foreign ownership, control and influence, to guide industry on those types of risks.

Senator PATERSON: So the minister or the department haven't exercised their powers, even for the SoNS, or Systems of National Significance—the systemically important critical infrastructure operators—when it comes to these apps?

Mr Hansford : No, because the direction powers in section 32 of the act are premised on an adverse security assessment. So the department hasn't used directive powers—and they're the minister's directive powers—because the prerequisite has not been met. But the way we tackle vendor risk is by requiring, in the 13 classes of infrastructure assets, a risk management program and mitigation of supply risks. One of the supply risks relates to vendors.

Senator PATERSON: Yes, but as you yourself said, specific action was required about these apps because of the extreme risk to the government. I think it would flow logically that extreme risk also exists for providers of critical infrastructure, given the public assessments that ASD and others have made about the intentions of foreign governments, including the Chinese government, to seek to establish a dormant presence on those networks for the purposes of future sabotage. We shouldn't make their task any easier by using software that they have control over. You're right: it was AGD that issued the PSPF direction about TikTok, so it wasn't your responsibility at the time, and it would have been their responsibility to write to critical infrastructure, I guess. Given that you've now written to critical infrastructure operators about these two apps, will you consider writing to them about TikTok as well?

Mr Hansford : I believe—I'm just recalling: I had the function in 2023—we had a discussion with infrastructure, but I'll consider writing to them formally.

Senator PATERSON: When you say 'a discussion with infrastructure', do you mean the department of infrastructure, or do you mean infrastructure providers?

Mr Hansford : The department, at that time, managed critical infrastructure, including those entities regulated under the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act. And I believe we did have a discussion at the time. I'll just refresh my memory, given that it was two years ago.

Senator PATERSON: I think there are something like 200 SoNS. There would probably be, what, 3,000 critical infrastructure providers overall? How did you have a discussion with all of them simultaneously?

Mr Hansford : We do lots of town halls, and we have a trust and information sharing network. That has a couple of thousand people. The way in which I communicate en masse is with our Critical Infrastructure Advisory Council, which has a representative from each of those different sectors, and they cascade that information down in some ways. In other ways I write to them.

Senator PATERSON: Okay. Could I ask you to, on notice, consider whether sufficient communication has been provided about the extreme cybersecurity risks of TikTok and, if you think it's not sufficient, that you address it?

Mr Hansford : Certainly.

Senator PATERSON: Moving on to another topic, I have some questions about Sayet Akca. In media reports he is being referred to as an alleged mastermind behind the Dural caravan incident. I don't want to ask any questions about his involvement in the Dural caravan incident, because I'm mindful of your advice about that earlier, Secretary and Minister, and I may pursue it with AFP, subject to time, this evening. But it has been publicly reported that he fled the country while on bail. Is that correct, to your knowledge?

Ms Foster : We're just trying to establish where in the organisation that knowledge would reside. But the short answer is that we can't comment on individual cases.

Senator PATERSON: Whose responsibility is it for ensuring that someone on criminal charges is not able to leave the country?

Ms Foster : I think this line of questioning might go better in outcome 3, with the ABF. My instinct is that that's more a policing matter, but I'd like my Border Force colleagues to be able to contribute.

Senator PATERSON: I will be interested to pursue that with them as well, but I want to understand about your state of knowledge about this. Have you been briefed about Mr Akca's departure from Australia?

Ms Foster : I'm aware of it. I'm trying to recall in what circumstances and how. Let me take that on notice and see if my office can help.

Senator PATERSON: It is alleged that he departed by boat while he was on bail for drug offences. I think two people have now been charged with facilitating his departure: a German national Thomas Goertz and an Australian Sean Ryan. They were in court last week. Do you have any knowledge about those charges?

Ms Foster : I'm aware of them and I will ask the relevant officers to be prepared in outcomes 2 and 3.

Senator PATERSON: In what respect would it fall under outcome 2, for my background?

Ms Foster : I am aware of the issue, I just can't recall the circumstances and the engagement that the departments had. Let me ask those officers to let me know where we can best address that.

Senator PATERSON: The chair has been clear about us asking questions in the relevant outcomes today and the limited time we have for each outcome. I don't want to find out when we get to outcome 2 or 2 that I should have asked this in outcome 1. I may not be able to address that.

Ms Foster : Absolutely. I'm expecting folks will be doing that right now so they can tell me where best to direct this.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. I'll move onto another matter while that happens. This is about terrorism listings; I think that will fall under you again, Mr Smyth. Since the listing of Ansar Allah last year, the Houthis, has the Department of Home Affairs undertaken any work on other terrorist listings?

Mr Smyth: We always have under review the possibility of looking at organisations to be listed whether they would meet a particular threshold or not. That is a constant piece of work we have under active review.

Senator PATERSON: Are there any groups you are looking at right now that could require a listing in the next six weeks, noting we may enter caretaker mode shortly?

Mr Smyth: I think I referred to this in my evidence to you a month ago that it is a longstanding practice of government that we don't discuss who may be considered for a listing.

Senator PATERSON: I didn't ask who, I just asked whether.

Mr Smyth: We don't discuss 'whether' either, or what number of organisations, or what organisations. I'm not able to go to that detail.

Senator PATERSON: What would the process be if you did believe a terrorism listing was necessary in caretaker, given the role of ministers in listing terrorist organisations?

Mr Smyth: We would follow the caretaker conventions.

Senator PATERSON: What are they?

Mr Smyth: The conventions would potentially require both sides of politics to be considered and engaged in terms of whether or not a listing was going forward because it requires ExCo consideration at the end of the day.

Ms Foster : Mr Smyth is reflecting the fact that the government, if we made an assessment that it was a significant issue, would need to consult the opposition.

Senator PATERSON: Some of these listings have taken quite a lot of time—weeks and weeks of ministerial consideration. If there were a need to list an organisation in the circumstances of a federal election, I would hope it would be more prompt than that. I will request in the usual way—as oppositions do—a briefing once we do enter caretaker mode formally. Does the department undertake to brief me on other potential listings at that time?

Ms Foster : The department would brief the minister, and it would be the minister's call on how to engage with the opposition.

Senator PATERSON: Even under the caretaker provisions, you wouldn't brief the opposition about a pending or possible terrorism listing that may require opposition support during a caretaker period?

Ms Foster : I'm not saying we wouldn't; I'm saying that process is done through the minister.

Senator PATERSON: That seems like a conditional answer to me. Last year, former minister O'Neill sat on the advice from the department to list the Houthis for a period of six weeks and then the Prime Minister also waited a further four weeks before writing to first ministers on the listing, so it delayed the listing quite considerably. Is it normally the Prime Minister who writes to first ministers about a terrorism listing?

Mr Smyth: Yes, it is.

Senator PATERSON: It hasn't previously been either the Attorney-General or Minister for Home Affairs who's written?

Mr Smyth: I'll get my colleague Ms Smyth to go through the details of how the listing process actually works.

Ms Smyth : Historically, both the PM and the Attorney have written to first ministers in the context of listing of organisations.

Senator PATERSON: Did the Minister for Home Affairs do that previously when they were the responsible minister?

Ms Smyth : I'll have to take that on notice just to be sure that's correct.

Senator PATERSON: It's my recollection, having sat on a few parliamentary inquiries into terrorism listings, that under the former government, when the home affairs minister was responsible, it was the home affairs minister who wrote to their counterparts at the state level. Under what circumstances does the Prime Minister take that responsibility from the relevant minister?

Ms Smyth : That's a matter for the Prime Minister.

Senator PATERSON: Doesn't the act require that the responsible minister write to their counterparts?

Ms Smyth : The act does require that. It is for the Attorney, who is responsible for the listings and the regulations, to determine who is best to write to first ministers.

Senator PATERSON: Why in the instance of the Houthis was it the Prime Minister who did so?

Ms Smyth : I would have to defer to the Department of the Prime Minster and Cabinet on that.

Senator PATERSON: Right. Can you tell me of other terrorism listings? Has it been the Prime Minister or the Attorney who has written?

Ms Smyth : Historically, I would have to take that on notice. I don't have that information here.

Senator PATERSON: You don't have any memory of the Prime Minister having done so on any other occasion?

Ms Smyth : I don't. I've been in the role for 12 months and, in that time, no. Historically, I am not aware, but I could take that on notice.

Senator PATERSON: I'm not either. Mr Smyth, in your experience, is it common for the Prime Minister to take this responsibly?

Mr Smyth: Again, I would have to defer to my colleague, take that on notice and go through the details.

Senator PATERSON: You can't think of another instance?

Mr Smyth: I'm not aware at this particular point. I think that in my time the organisation that we listed last year was obviously the Houthis. I believe that is the one that has been listed during my time in this role.

Senator PATERSON: Yes; I'm not aware of any examples either where a prime minister has done so, so I'm interested in understanding how the decision was made. The department has no visibility on how that decision was made?

Mr Smyth: If we can go back and check our records, we'll take that on notice.

Senator PATERSON: How would a decision like that be made?

Mr Smyth: I would imagine that there are deliberations that occur between various ministers and the Prime Minister's Office as to the process. Given that we have letters going out to first ministers, it may well have been the case that the Prime Minister rather than the Attorney was effectively writing out to premiers and chief ministers, but, again, I will take that on notice.

Senator PATERSON: So it's not a change to the process that's been made permanently going forward?

Mr Smyth: Again, can I take that on notice in terms of how that occurs? What actually happens is that the Minister for Home Affairs writes to the Attorney-General, providing a listing for consideration. The Attorney-General then effectively takes the process from that particular point. It would really be more a matter for the Attorney and the Prime Minister, so it may well be better directed towards the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet and the Attorney-General's portfolio.

Senator PATERSON: This listing took an extra ordinarily long period of time compared to other recent new listings. The department raised the listing, according to their submission, to the PJCIS on 17 January. AGS provided advice to Home Affairs on 30 January. Home Affairs provided a submission to the minister on 31 January. It wasn't till 13 March, six weeks later, that the home affairs minister wrote to the Attorney-General. That is six weeks of ministerial consideration, which is the longest I've been able to find for any recent terrorism listing. Are you aware of a longer period of ministerial consideration than that?

Mr Smyth: Again, I would have to check my records.

Senator Watt: My recollection is that this has been gone over in some detail at previous hearings. I can't remember the reasons that were given around those timeframes, but I do remember that reasons were given, so it might be helpful to refer back to that previous evidence as well.

Senator PATERSON: The Attorney-General wrote more promptly about this and acted more promptly on it. There was less delay by the Attorney-General. But it was on 20 March that the Attorney agreed to the listing and wrote to the Prime Minister, but then it wasn't until 18 April that the Prime Minister wrote to first ministers. What was happening in that time? Did the Prime Minister need to receive advice? Did the department provide advice to the Prime Minister about the listing? Why was there a four-week delay?

Mr Smyth: I would have to refer you to the Attorney-General's portfolio and the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet in relation to that, Senator.

Senator PATERSON: After the PM wrote to first ministers, in varying timeframes they wrote back to him and didn't object to the listing. That meant that it didn't go to EXCO until 23 May. This was a terrorism listing of an active terrorist organisation that our allies had listed that took four months from start to finish. What guarantees do we have that the next terrorism listing will be faster than this one?

Senator Watt: Before the officials answer—and I'm happy for them to answer—I think the broader point that should be made is that we do take these issues seriously. We are thorough in our assessment of them. That prevents us making stupid mistakes like claiming that incidents on the US-Canada border are terrorist incidents when they're not and like running around for weeks beating up an alleged terror incident that turns out to be a hoax. Actually getting it right can be important, and sometimes that takes a bit of time. The alternative is making stupid mistakes with national security, and that's not the approach of this government.

CHAIR: I was due to hand the call over. I'll give you a chance to have your question—

Senator PATERSON: I think the officials haven't had a chance to respond to my question.

CHAIR: Yes, sorry.

Mr Smyth: I would echo the minister's statements. We take our responsibilities here very seriously. We do so in a very diligent manner to ensure that we have met all of the criteria and that we're very confident that a determination can be made in relation to this. At times, there are pieces of correspondence and questions being asked that we are required to follow up on. But as to giving a definitive time into the future, that would be very difficult for us because it obviously relies on other parties making decisions and as to whether or not they make those considerations in a particular timeframe.

Senator PATERSON: I don't doubt that you take that seriously and that you are very diligent, but the record shows that you were able to move much more quickly—and your counterparts in AGD and AGS were able to move much more quickly—than the ministers were. Was it unclear to them that the Houthis were a terrorist organisation, and six weeks and then four weeks were required to determine that they were, even though your advice was clear?

Mr Smyth: I'm not privy to some of those considerations that go on in ministers' offices.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Ghosh, you have the call.

Senator GHOSH: I've got some questions in relation to counter foreign interference and counterterrorism. They relate to the Centre for Counter-Terrorism Coordination and the Counter Foreign Interference Taskforce. I understand that the government made the Counter Foreign Interference Taskforce permanent. Are you able to elaborate on the significance of that permanence and an ongoing funding allocation?

Mr Smyth: Yes. The funding was made last year, in last year's budget. I think there was $71.6 million allocated to foreign interference. One of the key centrepieces of that was making the funding for the Counter Foreign Interference Taskforce ongoing. That is, obviously, critical in terms of ongoing investigations and having dedicated resources focused by those intelligence and national security organisations on the threat of foreign interference. I think Director-General Burgess is on the record as saying that the level of espionage and foreign interference in Australia is extreme and is predicted to get worse. That level of funding that applies to the foreign interference taskforce enables it to meet its remit to start to deal with that threat.

Senator GHOSH: Director-General Burgess will appear before us later today, but in the context of that increase in foreign interference and concern around espionage, what would be the impact of a 20 per cent reduction in funding to the taskforce in your view?

Mr Smyth: The Department of Home Affairs is not a member of the taskforce. The taskforce is led by ASIO and the AFP with a number of other organisations. I think that question is best directed to them.

Senator GHOSH: May I ask about the University Foreign Interference Taskforce and if you have an update or any information you can share in relation to its more recent activities.

Mr Smyth: Yes, we met. I think 13 March was our last meeting. I'm just checking my brief for the last meeting. I'm pretty sure that close to 13 March was the most recent UFIT meeting. We have been focused on quite a body of work with the universities that are engaged in that, particularly around the Group of Eight and Universities Australia. We've had a number of working groups. We've conducted a number of tabletop exercises with the universities.

We've also been getting a number of case studies together with the university sector so that we're able to better position real-life examples of foreign interference in the university sector in research and academia that are translatable across the sector so that academics, researchers, faculty members and administrators at universities are very much aware of the threat of foreign interference, what it can potentially look like and some of the mitigation strategies that they're able to put in place to counter the effects of foreign interference. There are a number of meetings that go off the back of that. We have a range of guidelines that we've provided to the sector as well that have been reviewed and updated. Also, we've provided guidance as to foreign interference activities against student activities on campus, in terms of protests et cetera, that have been updated and provided to the sector.

Senator GHOSH: Mr Blackman, did you want to add anything?

Mr Blackman : I can confirm 13 March was the last time we had a UFIT meeting.

Senator GHOSH: In light of the observations you made about the trends in foreign interference and overseas espionage in Australia, are you able to offer any insight or update in relation to the trends on university campuses?

Mr Smyth: I think it's fair to say that, consistent with Director-General Burgess's comments, we are concerned about the level of potential foreign interference and cyber and espionage activities that occur against this sector. There are critical pieces of technology that are being researched at and developed on a number of university campuses, and we take the role very seriously in terms of working with the sector to ensure that they are very much aware of how they can harden their environment and what mitigation treatments they can put in place in relation to that.

Recently, Minister Burke launched what is called TechFIT, which is the Technology Foreign Interference Taskforce that Mr Hansford's area is responsible for. As part of that meeting, we agreed that, once a year, we would combine the UFIT and TechFIT meetings—because, obviously, a lot of technology companies are either funding research or are the beneficiaries of a lot of that research—to ensure that we're as linked up as we can be. It was clear at that TechFIT meeting that there is still a bit of a way to go in terms of educating the sector, particularly new technology companies and the like, about some of the threats of foreign interference. We believe that researchers at universities, faculty members et cetera will be able to work in collaboration with TechFIT to ensure that we've got a more holistic, joined-up approach to hardening the environment.

Senator GHOSH: Are you able to give us a quick update on the activities that the Centre for Counter-Terrorism Coordination have been undertaking?

Mr Smyth: I'll pass that to Ms Smyth. She is responsible for the centre.

Ms Smyth : There has been a lot on in my division, but most recently there was the launch of the new Counter-Terrorism and Violent Extremism Strategy: A Safer Australia. The funding of $106 million and some ongoing funding for critical countering violent extremism programs has been a welcome addition to the work of the centre. We are setting about implementing the strategy. There are 23 action items under the strategy, and 19 have commenced. We have a range of actions that my team are working through that cover awareness raising, education and support services to the communities, supporting and increasing capabilities of those who are responsible for countering violent extremism programs, enhancing our national approaches to assist individuals disengaging from a pathway of radicalisation, and strengthening our technological capabilities. Also, we're doing a significant amount of work with industry, international and like-minded partners to draw from their learnings and their lessons and work with them.

I regularly bring the domestic community together, as does the CT coordinator—they're the state and territory counterparts responsible for law enforcement and first ministers' departments—to regularly discuss our domestic situation. I'm responsible for the provision of funding for counter-terrorism capability domestically as well. There's $18 million every year set aside for a special fund to fund, improve and lift counter-terrorism capability within Australia. I could talk for a long time, but if you want to—

Mr Smyth: The other key thing is that we held the Australia-New Zealand Counter-Terrorism Committee meeting, which we host every six months. That was held last Friday in Sydney.

Senator GHOSH: Are you able to give us an update or an indication perhaps on some of our partners that you referred to and what they're doing by way of resourcing countering violent extremism within their own populations? Are they increasing resources? Are people keeping it at about the same? Are people reducing the funding they're giving?

Ms Smyth : It's a bit of all columns, which is potentially an unhelpful answer. But most definitely our like-minded partners are seeing very similar challenges, particularly those articulated by the Director-General of ASIO in February. It's an increasingly challenging environment. The trajectory does appear to be trending upwards in that there are more significant challenges in our community. We are seeing increases to radicalisation, with individuals radicalising more quickly. Our partners are seeing very similar. The challenges in relation to our online environment is something shared by our partners and the complexity of addressing those issues. So all partners are currently working very hard to try and respond to current risks and threats, noting that the trajectory appears to look as though it's going to increase.

Senator GHOSH: If that trajectory is increasing, what would you say would be the impact of a 20 per cent reduction in the funding to the centre and the implementation of the strategy?

Mr Smyth: I would say that, as per Mr Hansford's answer earlier, we work within the budget that is provided to us by government. The priorities by government drive our considerations as to where we place those resources. That's the way that I've certainly operated throughout my Public Service career.

Senator GHOSH: Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Shoebridge.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I asked some questions earlier about the process for Kaspersky Lab and DeepSeek, and I think you said they both represent extreme risk. Just for the purposes of the committee understanding what the nature of that risk is, can you identify, in relation to each of those platforms, what the nature of the extreme risk was?

Mr Hansford : Certainly. On Kaspersky, it was actually subject to correspondence to non-corporate Commonwealth entities in 2017, I believe. Effectively the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, at that time, wrote to all agencies. We, in our compliance work in Mr Neal's team, saw that particular vendor being used, I think, in one of the supply chains of a department, and we thought it was important, given the previous actions by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, to put on the record that that is already banned. So that was the driver for that particular direction—and given the ability and the intelligence behind that vendor. On DeepSeek—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I should have asked them one at a time. In relation to Kaspersky, though, it was banned from US government platforms three years ago, can you explain why there was a three-year delay between the US acting and Australia acting?

Mr Hansford : Australia, at the Australian government level, acted in 2017, and we reconfirmed in 2025 through a formal direction. That direction's power was only extant since 2023.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Alright. So there was a memo that went out in 2017—is that right?

Mr Anstee : It was a letter from the secretary of Prime Minister and cabinet.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Did that oblige all agencies to have no dealings and to remove all Kaspersky software off their systems? Did it apply to them, too?

Mr Hansford : That's right. The letter effectively said for non-corporate Commonwealth entities to not use Kaspersky products.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Can you provide a copy of the letter to the committee?

Mr Hansford : We'll take that on notice.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Then there was the powder to issue directions given in 2023.

Mr Hansford : That's correct.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: And then the direction was made in 2025.

Mr Hansford : That's correct. I also wrote in 2024—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: In the meantime, in 2022, the US—let me finish—issued an official banning notice in 2022; is that right?

Mr Hansford : I think that's right. The only addition is in 2024 I wrote to a range of chief security officers also outlining the threat and the previous advice by the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: What are the risks from Kaspersky? What are the extreme risks?

Mr Hansford : There are a range of risks, some of which rely on classified intelligence. Effectively, they go to foreign ownership control and influence, the ability for an actor to conduct things like cybersecurity vulnerabilities about the security settings behind the product itself. There are a range of different settings.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: In common parlance, it potentially has backdoors for foreign players to come in, get behind cybersecurity protections, snoop on what's being done—those are the nature of at least a subset of the risks; is that right?

Mr Hansford : There are potential vulnerabilities. I think Senator Polley asked about edge devices last Senate estimates, and that's an example of some of the threats, yes.

Mr Anstee : An additional key consideration is under the legal powers of the jurisdiction where an organisation may reside—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: They can be forced to disclose information.

Mr Anstee : the state can compel data release or certain behaviours by the company.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: If the action in 2017 was effective, there would have been no Kaspersky Lab products anywhere in the Commonwealth suite of agencies and corporate and non-corporate entities. But obviously something prompted the most recent action. What prompted the most recent action?

Mr Hansford : The issue that prompted the 2024 email from me to chief security officers was, as I said, a detection of its use in the supply chain of one government agency. So that prompted re-enlivening and drawing people's attention to that 2017 correspondence. The secretary made the decision to issue a formal direction in relation to Kaspersky.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: And that direction happened in late February?

Mr Hansford : That's right.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Do we know when? I thought it was the 26th, but I could be wrong; it may have been earlier.

Mr Neal: It was 21 February.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: So it was because you became aware of it being used in the supply chain. Have you undertaken an audit to identify where it has been used across the government since that time?

Mr Neal: We conducted our survey in late 2024, which did lead to the considerations of the government security committee and the protective security board, and, for all non-corporate Commonwealth entities, it requested them to scan their environments and their policies around Kaspersky Lab.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Did it find multiple uses of the product or products?

Mr Neal: Through that survey, plus engagements with critical infrastructure in states and territories, there were multiple instances of Kaspersky labs being included across those three cohorts.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Can you identify how many?

Mr Neal: I don't have that number in front of me, but I would say there were multiple.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Has there then been an audit done to see if any of those extreme risks that caused the banning notice had actually eventuated in relation to any of the use of the Kaspersky Lab's products? Have you gone through and done that audit?

Mr Neal: There is a requirement within the direction itself to report on completion. At the completion of that and the completion of the three directions from July, which also have audit requirements, we'll have a complete picture of the environment within the Commonwealth, and we'll be able to make an assessment on access.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I assume multiple agencies have used product from Kaspersky Lab. Do I understand that to be correct?

Mr Neal: There were multiple instances across the three cohorts, which was the Commonwealth government, the states and territories, and critical infrastructure.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Were there multiple instances in the Commonwealth space?

Mr Neal: There was one instance that I'm aware of within potential procurement, and there was another instance that I'm aware of of access to Kaspersky Lab.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: And then there were multiple other instances at a state and territory level in addition to that.

Mr Neal: Yes.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Is there an audit being done to see whether or not the extreme risks which led to the banning did eventuate in either of those two Commonwealth incidences?

Mr Neal: In those individual incidences, we did engage with both organisations to assure us that there wasn't undue access, and we have engaged with our technical authority partners as well. The survey, in one instance, found it to be relatively light access, and the second was a potential procurement process.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Was there an audit done to ensure that there was no inappropriate access? That's a simple question.

Mr Neal: There were engagements. I wouldn't say 'audit'.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Engagements?

Mr Neal: We engaged with the organisation, who then did an inspection within their organisation.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Alright. Do you think, in hindsight, given that the risks were identified in 2017 and that the US acted in 2022, that you could've taken action? These were, obviously, identifiable risks. Should action have been taken earlier? Are there any lessons to learn from this?

Mr Neal: It's important to recall that, in July 2024, we issued a series of directions to speak not just to the specific problems with Kaspersky Lab but the issue writ large of foreign ownership control and influence across technology assets. What we did there was issue a direction for a technology asset stocktake for internet connected devices across the Commonwealth and then issue a separate direction relating to procurement around foreign ownership control and influence such that, essentially, agencies and departments are on notice both to report to Home Affairs all their internet connected devices and to contemplate foreign ownership control and influence risk as they manage their technology estate.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: We might just go through the same process on DeepSeek, then. When was the banning notice issued in relation to DeepSeek?

Mr Neal: On 4 February.
