Senator PATERSON: Yes, just once. So the minister hasn't asked for an update on how this is going?

Mr Burke : We haven't provided, to my recollection, written updates, but there certainly have been conversations with ministers going back into 2024. There were fairly routine, I think, updates. That's part of the CSO updates.

Ms Foster : I think Ms Sharp can help too.

Ms Sharp: I think, as you're thinking about the role the FFA plays in the CSO scheme, what the FFA can be used for is to make clear who the specified authority is for the purpose of monitoring the conditions. As Mr Burke outlined, that specified authority can be either a state based body or a Commonwealth one. Depending on the state of negotiations or whether there's an FFA in place at the time we're ready to apply for one in a jurisdiction, we make the decision about whether we go with the state—so, if we were to apply for one now in New South Wales, New South Wales would perform that function. If the negotiations aren't sufficiently progressed with a particular state, we have a couple of options. One of the options is that the Commonwealth does it through a combination of Border Force, AFP and possibly contracted service providers, depending on the nature of the conditions. The other is that, if it were a detention order, we could seek New South Wales agreement to move the person to New South Wales for that detention. Senator PATERSON: So the delays in securing a community safety order have nothing to do with the lack of conclusion of FFAs?

Ms Sharp: Nothing at all.

Senator PATERSON: If it were the case that you had an applicant who was ready to proceed with—in Victoria, say, where there's no agreement—there'd be no hesitation in applying?

Ms Sharp: Well, we would need to be clear, when we apply to the court, who the specified authorities are. But, as I said, we are working on options so that we can progress either way—which would be a contracted service provider for a supervision order—

Senator PATERSON: Not for law enforcement, presumably.

Ms Sharp: No. For a lot of these functions we're talking about, the conditions don't require a police officer. They could be a community health provider, or someone like our SRSS provider, who provides other supports, could be contracted to do some of that servicing.

Senator PATERSON: Sure, but obviously the reason why you're having these negotiations with the states at all is that they have state police forces, and the state police forces are much larger than the Federal Police and have much more presence on the ground in the states and territories than the AFP has, so they're better placed to enforce these, aren't they?

Ms Sharp: It's partly to do with the size. Many of them are running big schemes that are state based schemes. So it's not that we need a really large service for one or two people; it's that they have an existing service footprint and it seems efficient to use theirs.

Senator PATERSON: Sure. So the AFP is equally well placed to provide the law enforcement required on an NZYQ person?

Mr Burke : It's not about the law enforcement. As Ms Sharp just said, it's really more about economies of scale.

Ms Foster : But I think it's fair to say that the reason we're pursuing the FFAs is that that is our preferred option.

Senator PATERSON: Indeed.

Ms Foster : What Ms Sharp is saying is that, if we don't have that or we don't yet have it, we are able to proceed.

Senator PATERSON: I hear that. What I'm trying to understand is why it's your preferred option. I would have thought—but it is very open to someone to correct me if I'm wrong—that one of the reasons why is the coverage and the presence that state police forces have for that law enforcement component.

Mr Burke : No, I don't think that really is the reason. Particularly around services that hitherto the Commonwealth has not provided and where a state already has existing contractual arrangements, existing expertise and potentially a greater economy of scale, it's more about making use of infrastructure that already existing rather than duplicating it. Senator PATERSON: Help me understand. If there's a breach of a CSO condition, you're saying that the AFP, which is a tiny fraction of the size of a state police force let alone all of them, is equally well placed to enforce that in a state and territory, as a state police force is?

Senator POLLEY: I just wanted to investigate a little bit more the modernisation around our border. If you could, give me some figures in relation to the total full-time equivalent positions that have been working in relation to the incoming passenger card. Who has been working on that?

Ms Spencer : The background to this is that, as you know, the yellow incoming passenger card is what we use currently to collect information. It's collected on behalf of a number of agencies across the Australian government. During the COVID pandemic, there were a number of efforts that were undertaken to improve that and digitise it to ensure that we had information in advance of people arriving at the border. That then helps us target interventions once people actually arrive at the border. For more details, I might get Ms Tharanie Vithanage, First Assistant Secretary, Strategy and Policy, up to the table to support as well.

Senator POLLEY: Thank you.

Ms Vithanage : In terms of the steps leading up to it, we've also had the support of Qantas and Brisbane Airport to help us with the product itself. The previous iteration, as Ms Spencer has already outlined, was the yellow card, which we have been trying to get rid of for some time now. In terms of progress coming forward, recently, on the 12th of this month, we actually had Qantas flights coming from LAX to Brisbane Airport included in the trial, and, on 19 March, all Qantas flights coming into Brisbane Airport were included in the trial. Senator POLLEY: What are the benefits in relation to border force and also for those who are lucky enough to be flying in and out of Brisbane?

Ms Vithanage : The benefits for both the Australian Border Force and to the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry are that we get the information up to 72 hours ahead of time. It also allows us to provide information to travellers that helps them make a decision perhaps not to bring items in, because they've got the time to make that decision. And then, as passengers make the declaration and move through our clearance processes, it just makes their experience seamless but also allows us to interact with only those passengers we need to—for example, those who have made declarations or those we have a concern about.

Senator POLLEY: Have there been any other attempts to modernise and introduce a digital card like this?

Ms Vithanage : There have been attempts in the past, and Ms Spencer referred to the health declarations that were in place during the pandemic itself. But there are a lot of agencies involved in the Incoming Passenger Card, so we have been working for some time to try and modernise it.

Senator POLLEY: Can you give us any information in relation to the Accenture card and the trials, and what happened with that program and that project?

Ms Vithanage : I'm not familiar with that particular card. Can you help me with the reference?

Senator POLLEY: My understanding was that the former government had a project. I think it was somewhere around $60 million invested, and I don't think it went anywhere. I'm just wonder if you had any information that you can enlighten us in relation to what happened with that program—

Senator SCARR: It sounds like you've got more information than the witness, Senator Polley.

CHAIR: She's very knowledgeable about this card.

Senator POLLEY: and what has changed now in relation to the success, which obviously has improved even since our last—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Constantly leaving Tasmania.

Senator POLLEY: Well, you from Victoria and New South Wales need one to get into Tassie. There are obviously learnings from the attempt and failure of the coalition to do this. What did you learn from that? And was it $60 million that was actually invested?

Ms Vithanage : I'd have to take the exact amount on notice. I think you're referring to what we would refer to as the Digital Passenger Declaration, the DPD. As you have already mentioned, it was built during the pandemic as a tool that we were seeking to collect compulsory health and vaccination information from. It was a standalone app, which is quite different to what we're offering from the Australia Travel Declaration perspective. The other bit to this is the involvement of Qantas in integrating it into their frequent flyer app. So we've certainly learnt from the mistakes that we had made, particularly around the standalone app component of it, to be able to integrate it into the passengers' experience.

Senator POLLEY: In relation to passengers—and you've said now it's been trialled for some time—what's the reaction from passengers?

Ms Vithanage : The reaction that passengers are having is really great to see. They're better informed but also have a much better experience going through the airport. Qantas have—in fact they were mentioning to me this week—had very little negative reaction to it. The ease of someone to be able to just complete an app on their phone as opposed to pulling out their glasses and their pencil after a flight of 13 hours or more has meant that we also get much better information and much better activity at the border.

Senator POLLEY: Is there a timeline for introducing this to other airports?

Ms Vithanage : There is. We're going to continue to work with both Qantas and our other industry counterparts to continue to roll this out.

Senator POLLEY: How is the Australian Border Force working with New Zealand, DAFF and other organisations and agencies to deliver the Incoming Passenger Card? Has there been advertising budget for this?

Ms Vithanage : I would have to take that question on the advertising budget on notice. I don't believe we have, other than using normal social media and media activity to better use the facility. Qantas have undertaken a fair amount of work, as you would appreciate, because it's on their app, in terms of both videos and other supporting material, including signage and so on, to be able to generate the maximum effect. I think the stats that were provided to me earlier this week were that about 50 per cent of eligible travellers are now starting to use that app so that's fabulous from a take-up perspective.

Senator POLLEY: How much time do you think that would take off passengers having to wait in line? Have you worked out the timeframe? When people come back from overseas, most people don't enjoy having to be in long lines. Is there any time saving there as well that you've identified?

Ms Vithanage : It's too early to tell in terms of the rollout that we have brought into place. We've been focusing on increasing the number of people who are using the app, including increasing it to groups as opposed to individual travellers. We will be in a position to assess the kind of data that you're after in due course.

Senator POLLEY: Do you have any data that shows the benefit of this, like people not bringing things in illegally? Has that actually been the data that's been collected thus far?

Ms Vithanage : Again, not yet. That's absolutely a question that we have interest in finding an answer to, as does DAFF from a prohibited-imports perspective, but we will be gathering that data over coming months.

Senator POLLEY: Do you see this as another important component of protecting our borders, with the benefits we will see over time? Are there going to be ongoing assessments of its success?

Ms Vithanage : Absolutely. This is just the start of a series of other traveller initiatives that allow us to focus on those passengers that we need to and allow legitimate travellers as seamless an experience as possible. But, obviously, we will need to continue to work with our counterparts in other agencies but also with industry to be able to land those future initiatives.

Senator POLLEY: For somebody who's not from an English-speaking background, is this easier for passengers to be able to do the right thing and be able to comply with our border requirements?

Ms Vithanage : That's certainly our intention, but, as you would appreciate, the Qantas app is in English. The accessibility requirements are appropriate for the users of that app. As we continue to roll this out and expand it beyond Qantas into a facility that all passengers can interact with, we would absolutely be cognisant of all those accessibility requirements, whether its culturally and linguistically diverse folk or folks requiring different types of access requirements to access it.

Senator POLLEY: Has there been any assessment about the financial benefits of making it easier for passengers to come in and to prevent people from bringing things into the country that they shouldn't be? Is there any dollar figure being put on that?

Ms Vithanage : Not that I've seen, but it's undeniable in terms of efficiency, by encouraging the type of behaviour that we want and stopping people from bringing in the wrong types of items but also increasing our ability to interact with them when they're actually at our border.

I don't think that would be a decision that binds a future government insofar as, if a future government came in and disagreed with that, it would be quite straightforward to simply withdraw the matter from the court. Senator PATERSON: Is the minister required to consult with the opposition before making that decision?

Senator POLLEY: I want to ask some questions in relation to the investment in immigration compliance functions for migrant workers that was undertaken after the Nixon review. When we came into government, it was pretty obvious that the system was broken, so there's been an investment. Considering that the Leader of the Opposition oversaw that department for some six years, I'd like to find out a bit more about how that investment has changed things around and what the compliance functions are.

Mr Thomas : You are correct that the department received an additional $50 million over four years from the 2023-24 budget that we are using for additional enforcement and compliance activities around migrant worker exploitation. That, combined with the outcomes of the Nixon review and other activities, means that we have been working extensively to strengthen our compliance regime and undertake a range of activities around migrant worker exploitation. One of the things we've been able to do is take previous Operation Inglenook, which was focused on noncompliance, migrant worker exploitation and identifying human trafficking and modern slavery within the sex industry, and expand that to all industries. So we've been undertaking much more activity in that space to broaden our activities to really identify and mitigate migrant worker exploitation. In addition to that, from 1 July last year, the strengthening employer compliance act came into force, which provided us with stronger enforcement abilities and outcomes against non-compliant businesses. Through our sponsor monitoring program we ensure that we are working with sponsors and with migrant workers to ensure they understand their obligations and taking enforcement action and compliance action where required—sanctions, fines, referral for prosecution et cetera. We've also undertaken a couple of pilots in the visa space: our strengthening reporting protections pilot, and our workplace justice visa pilot. Both two-year pilots commenced in July last year to enhance protections for individuals that may wish to report exploitation to make sure visas aren't unnecessarily cancelled where employers, for example, are threatening visa cancellation as a perverse consequence of reporting exploitation. The workplace justice visa pilot allows people to extend their stay in Australia to pursue workplace justice matters where they may have been exploited by an employer.

Senator POLLEY: With that $50 million additional resource, were there more people brought into the department to do this work or is this being undertaken by the same number of staff?

Mr Thomas : No. That $50 million allowed us to increase our staffing footprint in that compliance and enforcement space, which has allowed us to have more ABF officers out in the field undertaking these activities.

Senator POLLEY: How many officers do you have in the field?

Mr Thomas : For this financial year, our field operations and sponsor monitoring function has an ASL budget of 243.3 people. That workforce is spread across the country, undertaking those sponsor monitoring and field compliance activities.

Senator POLLEY: The work ensuring that compliance is working and people are not going to be exploited is pretty important work.

Mr Thomas : It is.

Senator POLLEY: Would you be able to do that if there were a cut to your resources?

Ms Foster : It would depend where those cuts were applied.

Senator POLLEY: Can you explain to me how having these functions actually protects our community?

Mr Thomas : These functions allow the department to do a range of things. Those functions in general undertake both community protection functions and functions that maintain the integrity of the migration system to ensure that, for example, we are locating and detaining unlawful noncitizens and other operational activity on top of the migrant worker exploitation activity. It's critical to ensure that we can identify these issues, mitigate them, refer them to other agencies, departments and law enforcement where required and start tackling and continue to tackle the really nefarious exploitation of the migration system if and where it's occurring.

Ms Foster : Senator, since Mr Thomas pulled this function together, he's had some really significant results in increased detentions and removals and has expanded the scope of where we're undertaking that activity so that we are able to send messages into the various parts of the system where there are unlawful noncitizens who should not be here anymore and start to progress their removal. We often find that when we put some focus on involuntary removals people start to move in a voluntary way, which is obviously a much more desirable outcome.

Senator POLLEY: What is the Sponsor Monitoring Unit, how many people are in it, and how does that actually work to protect these migrant workers?

Mr Thomas : I don't have the exact staffing number for the Sponsor Monitoring function specifically but, in a general sense, the Sponsor Monitoring Unit undertakes monitoring compliance and administrative activities regarding sponsorship obligations of standard business and temporary activity sponsors. So, they can bar or cancel a sponsor from engaging in the program where they identify exploitation, they can serve an infringement notice and they can issue a no-action letter, a compliance letter or an enforceable undertaking. They can pursue civil penalties, issue a prohibition declaration and refer individuals for visa cancellation, should it be a noncitizen undertaking these activities. They can also refer criminal matters to law enforcement for further action.

Senator POLLEY: Have you got any cases where employers have been in breach of compliance on more than one occasion?

Mr Thomas : I believe so. I would have to take on notice the exact numbers on how many repeat offenders there are, so to speak, but that certainly is my recollection. I'll take it on notice to check.

Senator POLLEY: Can you explain a bit more about what sorts of penalties can be applied against employers?

Mr Thomas : Regarding that list of activities I went through previously, I might explain the additional provisions from the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Employer Compliance) Act that came into force in July last year. That provided new criminal offenses for employers who coerced temporary migrant workers into working in breach of their visa conditions, so there are additional powers there. There's an additional mechanism for prohibiting an employer from employing additional temporary migrant workers if they have been found to be in breach of the laws. There were increased maximum criminal and civil penalties for work-related breaches of the act, expanded provisions for enforceable undertaking and issuing compliance notices, and the removal of disincentives for temporary migrant workers to report exploitation. So, there's quite a range of powers that they have access to in order to address any sponsor monitoring activities.

Senator POLLEY: How do you measure success in this immigration and compliance space?

Mr Thomas : In a few ways. Certainly just the amount of activity and engaging sponsors, in particular around educating them, providing information for both the sponsors and the workers. That can be quantified by numbers of visits, numbers of site visits and engagement activities as well as the number of notifications issued, whether it's a breach notice, a no-action letter and number of sponsors that have been sanctioned. As an example, in the financial year to 31 January, 134 sponsors were sanctioned. We served a number of infringement notices to the value of $63,000, but in previous years they've been as high as almost half a million dollars. We have issued 21 no-action letters and 151 breach notices. So, there's quite a range of activity to measure, but I think, in addition to that, that the qualitative feedback will be important as we engage with these areas, ensuring that awareness is increasing and people have a better understanding of both their obligations and their rights as employers and employees.

Senator POLLEY: As I understand, back in 2019, under the former government, the Migrant Workers' Taskforce had a number of recommendations. Have they been implemented?

Mr Thomas : Is this the Nixon review that you're talking about?

Senator POLLEY: Sorry?

Ms Foster : Is this the review that Christine Nixon did?

Senator POLLEY: No. This was the Migrant Workers' Taskforce to the former government in which they brought down recommendations in 2019.

Mr Thomas : I'm not familiar with that off the top of my head. I'd have to—

Have there been any other recent reports that temporary visa holders are using the protection visa pathway to be able to remain in Australia in order to continue working and that such cohorts may be taken advantage of? Can you tell me what strategies are being put in place to address this?

Mr Thomas : A few strategies across the department in the immigration compliance space are really focusing on the location, detention and removal of individuals that have failed the protection visa process, have no remaining pathways to remain in Australia and should depart. This is to ensure that, when someone concludes that process, they are encouraged to depart or removed as quickly as possible to disincentivise people making unmeritorious protection claims.

Ms Foster : That's one of the areas where we've seen some flow-on effect of the forced removals on people choosing to leave.

Ms Jeffery : I can give you data on that if you like.

Ms Foster : Yes. That'd be great, Sandra.

Ms Jeffery : Between 26 February 2024 and 31 January 2025, we detained 203 people in that circumstance where they were failed PV applicants and were in Australia unlawfully. CHAIR: I now welcome the Hon. Don Farrell representing the Attorney-General. Welcome, Minister. I also call officers from the Australian Federal Police. Minister, would you like to make an opening statement?

Senator Farrell: Thank you for the opportunity of making an opening statement. Given it's important the committee get an opportunity to ask as many questions as possible, I'm happy to defer that right and get into it.

CHAIR: Apologies, I should've welcomed the secretary; thank you for joining us. Commissioner, would you like to make an opening statement before we go to questions?

Mr Kershaw : Good afternoon, senators. Today I want to provide some practical information about the safety and protection of parliamentarians and high office holders for the weeks and months ahead. I have some sobering information I need to share, and at the end of this hearing I encourage you all to think about your plans for the upcoming poll and consider providing the AFP with relevant details so we can make informed decisions and provide you with necessary advice. The number of reports of threats to high office holders, federal parliamentarians, dignitaries and electorate officers continues to grow. In 2021-22 there were 555 reports, in 2022-23 there were 709 reports, in 2023-24 there were 1009 reports and this financial year as of 28 February 2025 there have been 712 reports. At this rate the number of threats this financial year will surpass those in 2023-24.

These numbers refer to the total number of threats and reports of harassment, nuisance and offensive communications reported to the AFP. It includes both direct and indirect threats relating to or reported by protected interests. The politicians who've been targeted are across the political spectrum, live throughout Australia and are of different backgrounds. A lot of these threats are directed at male politicians and high office holders. However, the nature of threats and comments directed at female parliamentarians and high office holders are particularly troubling. Australia's politicians and high office holders are being targeted because they have a public profile, because of comments they have made in the media or because of their positions on policy. However, in some cases it appears male offenders are targeting women because they are women or women with an ethnic background. The AFP will not tolerate this criminality and will take swift action.

While not all reports of crime will reach a criminal threshold and not all parliamentarians and not all high office holders will want us to lay formal charges, often they will ask us just to talk to the alleged offender. Noting that the AFP have a victim-centric approach, we'll often be guided by their wishes and deploy the blue uniform to knock on an offender's door. This can be enough to stop the harassment. Usually when we knock on their door they are shocked to see us (1) because they probably thought we could not identify them and (2) because they say they never meant to cause offence. In the past 13 weeks we have charged six men in five separate incidents for threatening parliamentarians and one man for allegedly threatening a political organisation. Their ages range from 29 years to 64 years.

While these are concerning statistics, our febrile environment in Australia is similar to many other democracies. COVID-19 contributed to a growing distrust of traditional institutions and polarised community views, and anonymising platforms have emboldened people to make comments and threats from a distance. In Australia we are recording an increase in issue motivated extremism and offenders who are quickly willing to use violence to further their cause. For those at the table today and more broadly across the parliament there is formal protective security advice in the Stay Secure booklet. We also provide advice on planned official engagements, which enables the AFP to assess whether a parliamentarian's activities may present an increased security risk. This is standard practice and will continue post election. Not all offices do this, but I encourage you all to consider the offer, because we need to work in partnership with you all. The closer we cooperate, the better the service the AFP will be able to provide.

The AFP has developed election-specific protected security advice. This has been prepared in consultation with key Commonwealth agencies and offers practical advice to address key campaigning risks for parliamentarians. This advice is available for parliamentarians and their staff to reinforce the importance of personal security as well as the reporting mechanisms for responses and intervention where required. Right now our security protection diplomatic liaison teams across the country are engaging with parliamentarians and their staff. The AFP has also established Operation AUSTRALIS25, which is supported by Commonwealth agencies and state and territory law enforcement partners to enable a coordinated rapid response for triaging, assessing and acting upon threats and reports of crime. An incident coordination centre will operate seven days a week and will manage all of the operations and information related to the federal election.

I know some of this information will be confronting to parliamentarians, staff and families. However, we need to provide the right education not just for victims but deter those who think it is acceptable to threaten politicians or high office holders. This goes to the heart of protecting our democracy and ensuring the cowards behind the correspondence do not silence the voices who serve and contribute to Australia. I wish you all a safe campaign, and we're now happy to take questions.

CHAIR: Thank you, Commissioner, for the work your officers do to keep parliamentarians and officeholders safe. We're very appreciative of the work and your teams. On indulgence I want to ask one question. From your language and your tone you seem pretty concerned about this escalation. Your advice to parliamentarians explicitly is to refer rather than not refer?

Mr Kershaw : We would prefer you to refer. It may be that you don't want to lay charges, but it paints a picture for us because that individual or individuals might have committed this four or five times. Then there are certain independent things we can do, whether it be to go and talk to that person or persons. The more information we get, the better we're able to provide the correct response.

CHAIR: Does that include electronic communications as well as other types?

Mr Kershaw : Especially electronic communications. You will get some vile threats. I've read some of them; they're absolutely horrific. We are pretty good at working out normally who has undertaken that and whether it's sitting in Australia or overseas, and that's why we work with overseas partners if it is coming from overseas.

CHAIR: Thank you for the work that you do. It sounds like an enormous amount of work that you'll undertake during the election itself.

Senator PATERSON: On behalf of the coalition can I add my appreciation as well for all the work that the AFP has already done in the space and what I know you and your offices will do over the next five or six weeks on behalf of the parliament and also on behalf of our democracy. It's unfortunate that so many resources from the AFP have to be deployed on threats like these, but that is the world we live in. You recognise the reality of that, and we're grateful for it.

Moving on to some other matters, the committee has just received correspondence from the Attorney-General making an application for public interest immunity, and it hasn't considered it yet. That's a matter for the committee, and I will leave the committee to resolve that at the first opportunity. But it only came in literally as we were sitting down to open up questions. Could you clarify for my benefit, given we've only just received the correspondence, what we can ask questions about and what you can answer questions about relating to the Dural caravan incident and what you cannot.

Mr Kershaw : I acknowledge we will be asked questions today regarding Operation Kissinger. Deputy Commissioner Barrett will provide some answers but will not provide information that risks an ongoing investigation. We have cited the minister's claim of public interest immunity on the basis of prejudice to the security and defence of the Commonwealth and of prejudice to Commonwealth and state relations. So the AFP will not be in a position to answer questions that may traverse that claim. Given continued leaks that have significantly impacted on this operation, we will be very firm on what information we will not provide. Senator PATERSON: On that last reference to leaks, obviously nothing you've provided in a public forum to the parliament is a leak. That's information put on public record. Any leaks that have happened about this investigation must have come from people familiar with the investigation, not members of this committee.

Mr Kershaw : No. But there are processes that, you would appreciate, have been undertaken in regard to that.

Senator PATERSON: I do appreciate that, and I do appreciate the damage that a leak can do. But answering questions from parliament about the conduct of the AFP is not a leak, and we have a task to do on behalf of taxpayers to ensure that the funds you administer achieve the objectives the government tasked you with, including keeping Australians safe. This was a serious incident that Australians have interest in. We do need to be able to ask questions, and I hope that, in answering those questions, you are guided by a principle of as much transparency as possible without jeopardising the investigation.

Mr Kershaw : Of course.

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. I assume, based on that PII letter—as I said, it's a matter for the committee to decide whether it accepts the claim are not—that questions about when or if the Prime Minister or ministers were briefed about this issue won't be answered by the AFP.

Mr Kershaw : That's correct.

Senator PATERSON: Can you explain why answering questions about that matter would be prejudicial to the investigation?

Mr Kershaw : I go back to the statement I just made.

Senator PATERSON: I do understand why was there a lot of reluctance about that at the last estimates, but, since the last estimates, there have been significant developments in the case, including people being arrested in connection with the investigation. The AFP and New South Wales police have put on public record at a press conference a higher degree of information about the case, none of which was asked about in the previous round of estimates and probably none of which I would have asked about in this round of estimates, had it not been public. Why is it that the AFP can disclose so much in a public press conference, along with New South Wales police, but not to a Senate committee?

Mr Kershaw : I can see how it would be of interest to the committee. For us, it goes back to, again, maintaining the independence of that investigation. Any problematic intersections within those investigations end up in court. I've seen it before, where some investigations are accidentally trampled on or interfered with and then you're in a scenario where the real criminals that we are after—the organised crime principals—have claims for legal challenge. We are quite sensitive to that, given the fact that the AFP doesn't take on a corner store thief or anyone like that. These are well-resourced organised crime targets who know our system very well and have tried to work out some of our tactics, so we're often loath to actually go down this path with anything that's active. If I were to disclose what is active, then that is intelligence that they will use against us in continuing to try to outwit and outplay the AFP and law enforcement.

Senator PATERSON: I certainly appreciate the seriousness of this investigation and the work that the AFP does, but I find one of the things you just said in your answer difficult to reconcile, which is that information that's provided could be used as part of a legal defence or to thwart an investigation or charges. You would know that evidence provided to the Senate in a committee hearing is protected by parliamentary privilege. It is inadmissible in a court hearing. It cannot be used as part of a defence.

Mr Kershaw : I understand that. I'm just reaffirming that this is the Attorney-General's claim.

Senator PATERSON: Yes, I do note that. I'll persist as best as I can in asking these questions, and we'll see how far we go. What can you tell me about Mr Sayet Akca, who has been publicly reported as the individual believed to be responsible for coordinating these attacks from offshore?

Ms Barrett : What might be helpful is if I go through the information that we are prepared to say publicly and see where we land at the end of that. To start with, in Sydney on 19 March, Assistant Commissioner Stephen Nutt and I met with the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, including Peter Wertheim and Alex Ryvchin. We provided them with more context about this crime, given that it is weighing very heavily on their community. We spoke about further opportunities, including how we as law enforcement can work together to tackle antisemitism. We continue to speak to a number of other Jewish organisations and also the government's Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, and I just want to thank them all for their support during this time.

I do note that you did, just now and earlier today, acknowledge that we went into quite a lot of detail about the incident when we held the media conference on 10 March this year. We really pushed the limits in our public statement about what we were prepared to say publicly during that conference, and the reason we pushed the limits so hard was that we knew how important it was to address multiple audiences, particularly the Jewish community who have been living in fear. That was the first and the last time that the AFP has publicly provided any operational information in relation to the operation. I don't intend to provide anything further today outside of what has already been said publicly, and that's because this, of course, is an ongoing investigation. There are some key pieces of information that I can reaffirm today that perhaps would be helpful.

I can reaffirm that, within hours of the caravan being found, any perceived threat was mitigated, and the investigation was referred to the New South Wales Joint Counter Terrorism Team. I can confirm that our experienced investigators almost immediately believed that the caravan was a fabricated terrorism plot. This was because of information that we already had, how easily the caravan was found, how visible the explosives were and that there was no detonator that was located, so the caravan was never going to cause a mass casualty event. I do want to say that the JCTT on multiple occasions up to the joint management committee, which is assistant commissioner level, discussed providing information to the public as early as we possibly could, noting the current environment. However, during our investigations, we did continue to receive tip-offs about other terror plots related to this matter, and I think you can understand that we do have to treat those at their highest out of an abundance of caution.

In terms of motive, we allege that a person offshore—a suspected criminal that is facing serious charges here in Australia—used local criminals to leverage the ongoing social-cohesion concerns in this country. We allege that this person paid local criminals to carry out antisemitic graffiti and vandalism for weeks whilst planning the caravan plot. We know that this was to create absolute fear and anxiety in the Jewish community to get attention from law enforcement. In exchange for providing information of an imminent threat they wanted to return to Australia without being sent straight to jail.

As I said during the media conference, regardless of the motivation of those responsible for this fake plot, this has had an absolutely chilling effect on the Jewish community. This twisted, self-serving criminality has no doubt terrified and terrorised Jewish Australians. What organised crime has done to the Jewish community is reprehensible. I said that on the day at the media conference. There was also unwarranted suspicion directed at other communities as well, which is also reprehensible. I want to say that using antisemitism or deploying antisemitic methods to get a deal with the Commonwealth will not work, and it is really despicable. In this case it's backfired on this individual. Today I call out this reprehensible plot for what it is: hateful, evil, offensive, and it weaponises antisemitism.

Finally, I want to say that this investigation was being progressed by the JCTT as a covert investigation until it was publicly disclosed by the Daily Telegraph on 29 January. That disclosure has had a significant detrimental impact on our ability to use our full suite of covert strategies and investigative capabilities to bring those responsible to justice. With every media article that's continued to draw this investigation out in the public domain, our members have had to quickly pivot and adapt their investigative strategies. I spent time with our investigators in Sydney last week. To say that they're very frustrated doesn't quite capture the mood amongst them. I want to take this opportunity to recognise how hard they've been working and what a great job they've done under such challenging circumstances.

Senator PATERSON: I appreciate that frustration on behalf of the team working on this. It would be very frustrating to have it disrupted in the way that it was. Ms Barrett : Again I'll just clarify: the joint counterterrorism team was. So four agencies including—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I fully accept the difficulties police have in circumstances where you have an ongoing investigation and you don't want to prejudice the investigation, but the difficulty from a parliamentary point of view and the public's point of view is that between 29 January and 10 March there was a vast amount of activity predicated on the story that was told by the Daily Telegraph on 29 January, which was that it was mass casualty risk and it was an antisemitic terror event. Mr Kershaw : My colleagues might correct me but, because it's a Joint Counter-Terrorism Team, there are agreed protocols. There are heaps of acronyms we use in policing all the time. Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I get that, but the Prime Minister said—and I'm not saying he said it with any malicious intent; I'm assuming that it was said in good faith—on 30 January:

Quite clearly this is aimed at terror …

Mr Kershaw : I don't agree with that assessment, and I think we have to go back to the claim that's been made.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: The public interest immunity claim?

Mr Kershaw : Yes.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Not only did the Prime Minister act on that misapprehension but we then had the federal parliament amending legislation about hate crimes to put in place mandatory sentencing based on that misapprehension. We had the New South Wales state parliament passing anti-protest laws based on that misapprehension. And all the time the AFP knew it was a misapprehension. You did not correct the public record.

CHAIR: Senator Shoebridge, I don't think you can speak on behalf of the entire parliament or the way that they were thinking about a certain piece of legislation.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: That was repeatedly referenced in the debate.

CHAIR: Yes, I'm just saying I don't think you can speak on behalf of the parliament.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Alright.

CHAIR: You do this quite often in estimates, particularly when the AFP is appearing before you. You make statements that are not correct or reflective of the facts. This is not a debate between you and the AFP. It is an opportunity for you to ask questions—

I am asking how you came to the conclusion.

Ms Barrett : I will restate what I said earlier: these are joint investigations. Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Did you turn your mind to those competing public interests? What was happening in parliaments—legal changes—based upon misapprehension by some if not all members of parliament, as against the impact on investigation? Did you turn your mind to that?

Mr Kershaw : Of course, but I would say that you have to remember that if any police officer who had access to that information were to then step out of bounds from the joint management committee—and that includes the commissioner; it doesn’t matter what rank you are, and you need to understand this, because this is what we do—you run the risk of attempting to pervert the course of justice, if you step out of line. That includes making certain public statements. You have to respect that process. It's been tried and tested in this country for 25 years, and it works. That was not part of any kind of strategy, and if it were they would be saying, 'Commissioner, we need to go public'—or commissioners, it would be, because it was a joint job. Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Commissioner, I'm not suggesting that this is a simple task. I think it's a very difficult balancing of public interest considerations. I'm not suggesting that it's simple; I'm asking whether you undertook that consideration.

Most of the deputy's team have been working seven days a week on this particular job. Our front end is pretty worn out at the moment, on this particular job and others. We're operating in a really complex environment.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Can I then come back to the question that I think would give the public far better understanding about how and why certain decisions were made. If you couldn't make a public statement, everybody is then asking—and I think they have a very reasonable basis to ask it—whether you gave a confidential briefing to the Attorney-General and the Prime Minister so that they, two of the most senior players in the space, knew what was happening and could direct the executive government and take their legislative roles forward knowing the proper context. That's why people keep asking.

Mr Kershaw : I'd like to help you but I'm not able to because of the PII claim.

Senator VAN: Commissioner, deputy commissioners and team, thank you for coming along. As always, it's appreciated, and we appreciate the work you do. I think your opening comments resonated with all of us. Commissioner, can I start with asking you about governance structures within the AFP.

Mr Kershaw : Sure.

Senator VAN: Can you describe what you view as the governance structures that hold the AFP accountable.

Mr Kershaw : The AFP Act governs our constitution and what we're set out to do and then the processes and procedures we have with making arrests and a whole range of things. I could talk all day about that, but we do have the chief operating officer here who might want to talk about the governance structures of police and, in particular, the AFP.

Ms Van Gurp : Can I clarify your question. Are you talking about our committee structures, our internal board structures, our commissioner's orders, our national guidelines—what part of governance? We have myriad.

Senator VAN: All companies have a board of directors, and the executive management and operation of any company is held accountable to that governance structure.

Ms Van Gurp : Our peak internal governance board is our strategy and performance board. That's chaired by our commissioner. Membership comprises myself, the deputy commissioners and a number of advisers at the national manager band 2 level. We have an independent audit and risk committee with three members that are independent of the AFP. The senior executives attend as advisers on that committee. That oversights all our audit and risk governance decisions and monitoring of our recommendations in that space. Underneath our strategy and performance board we have a range of specific boards. We have our enterprise operations board that I chair. That's where we focus on budget, resourcing and what not, the ICT-corporate side, and then we have our operational—

Ms Van Gurp : There's a lot of governance we do.

Senator VAN: The one that you referred to, I think it was the strategy and—

Ms Van Gurp : performance board.

Senator VAN: I appreciate that, and that's wonderful. I'm trying to test if there is any public accountability other than through this.

Ms Van Gurp : Senator, just to remind you and perhaps help you out, we're actually one of the most overseen agencies in the Commonwealth because we have both the law enforcement and the intelligence components. I'm trying to get a sense of your risk management, particularly around what you raised in your opening statement. I believe you talked about direct and indirect threats. Mr Kershaw : Sorry, what was that last bit?

Senator VAN: How does the AFP define 'threat'?

Mr Kershaw : It depends on what you're talking about. If you're talking about internal threats or external threats—they're two different things. Senator VAN: As I said, I was referring to how you were referring to threats in your opening statement. I assume that's criminal.

Mr Kershaw : For threats to parliamentarians, we collect intelligence. We gather that information and then work out whether or not the threat is credible and what actions are appropriate—or whether no actions are appropriate—for that particular threat.

Senator VAN: For those sorts of instances, are you able to provide on notice some definitions or something that we could work with to understand how you look at threats?

Mr Kershaw : Yes. Understanding that there is a wide range of slightly different meanings in the criminal world and understanding the other side of the business that we have, I'd be happy to.

Senator VAN: I understand that. What's the difference between a direct or an indirect threat and a direct and an implied threat?

Mr Kershaw : I'll take that on notice because I could probably speak about some of those where not everyone—

Senator VAN: We've got a couple of hours.

Mr Kershaw : I know, but not everyone would appreciate the different kinds of threats we have and how we treat those. So I'd probably want to take that on notice.

Senator VAN: So you can't give a simple split between direct and implied threats?

Senator VAN: Sure, but I'm asking you to simply separate out direct and implied or indirect threats.

Mr Kershaw : There are other methods. Do you want to talk about threats?

Ms Barrett : Again, it depends what type of threat we're talking about and which crime type we're talking about. So it's difficult to provide you with a specific answer to quite a general question.

Ms Gale : I would offer that the Protective Security Policy Framework outlines detail on threats and how they're assessed. Senator VAN: Do you offer parliamentarians secure briefings on those sorts of materials?

Ms Gale : We can do that, yes.

Senator VAN: That would be wonderful. I appreciate that. CHAIR: You have just two more minutes, Senator Shoebridge.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Right. I have a series of questions in relation to the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation. Mr Kershaw : Senator, if I could just assist. I've been on the record about this, about the tech companies needing to do more. This is a real sickness. Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I agree with you; the platforms should be a key target for this. CHAIR: I have to share the call. Senator Roberts.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you and your people for appearing here today, Mr Kershaw. According to our Commonwealth Constitution's opening sentence Australia is constituted as a Christian country. What's being done to charge those preachers in mosques of preaching hatred and threatening violence and use of physical force against Christians here in our country and bringing such hate preachers to justice?

Mr Nutt : Senator, I can take that one. Obviously, we're very concerned where online hate speech and other actions of hate occur in the community. We obviously work in partnership with our state and territory colleagues, who are often first responders to certain offences. The AFP does not monitor the internet. We certainly review any allegation that relates to hate speech targeting any protected group against the Commonwealth offences that are available to us and we assess the content in those circumstances. That often involves obtaining legal advice. These offences change over time, in terms of what an offence may look like, decisions of court and those sorts of things, so we always ensure that, at the time, we are looking at not only current but past conduct and that we evaluate that conduct against not only the offences but the standards and decisions of courts in the jurisdiction where the offences occurred.

Senator ROBERTS: Have any such preachers of hate in Australia been charged, and, if not, why not?

Mr Nutt : I don't have statistics relevant—

Senator ROBERTS: Can you get them?

Senator ROBERTS: Yes.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Chair, I have a point of order. CHAIR: Senator Shoebridge, thank you. You're welcome to go and post those thoughts on Facebook. Senator Roberts is able to make his views known, and people can take them at his word, knowing his past reputation for—I'm not saying that you are misleading the parliament, but you have your views and they're well known, and I think people can take your statements together with your previous statements. People can just read it. It's a document. I think we can move on. Senator Roberts, do you have any other questions?

Senator ROBERTS: Yes, I do. There have recently been faith based crimes committed in Australia involving fire bombings, graffiti painted on buildings, cars damaged and hate symbols displayed. How many arrests have been made, and what is being done to identify the criminals and bring them to justice?

Mr Nutt : Again, I'm happy to take those matters. Again, we can only speak on behalf of the AFP. Certainly, there are Commonwealth offences not only in the recent legislative amendment on 8 February, which has been described as the hate crimes bill, but other offences including in the prohibited hate symbols and other measures act. This legislation is available to our state and territory colleagues as well, and they can use those offences where state offences don't apply.

Since 8 January 2024, when the prohibited hate symbols act came into effect, we have not charged anyone in relation to prohibited Nazi symbols under 80.2H of the Criminal Code Act 1995; however, we have charged two individuals in respect of the prohibited terrorist organisation symbols—that is, the intentional public display of proscribed terrorism organisation symbols—and we've also issued a direction under section 80.2K for the display of a prohibited terrorist organisation symbol. We have not charged anyone in terms of the trading of symbols, but we do have a number of investigations on the books with respect to prohibited terrorist symbols generally.

In terms of advocating terrorism, which, again, is the current version of the offence which came into effect in December 2023, we haven't charged anyone. This is around advocating terrorism under section 80.2C of the Criminal Code. However, under the previous version, which was available between 2021 and 2023, we charged 10 persons for advocating terrorism under section 80.2C of the Criminal Code. As I mentioned, there was some updated hate crimes offences that came into effect on 8 February this year. Those offences are yet to be utilised by the AFP.

Senator ROBERTS: Minister, this question is for you. Will noncitizens convicted of hate crimes be subjected to deportation?

Senator Farrell: I'll have to take that question on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. Back to the AFP. Do AFP officers need to get permission from a higher authority before making an arrest, or may an AFP officer exercise their discretion to make an arrest for a crime unfolding in front of them?

Mr Kershaw : Normally, depending on the nature of the event—if it's a public order matter and some other particular matters—a senior officer can direct someone to be arrested, but there is also what we call the 'Office of Constable', which is an independent office that goes way back in the day to the UK, where an individual officer is held liable if they make the arrest. It's their decision, independent of anyone else. So you could have a situation where one officer may gather some facts and say, 'I'm okay to arrest that person,' and another officer may say: 'I'm going to use a summons. I'm not going to arrest them. I'm going to treat it differently or give them a caution.' We, as senior officers, have to respect that and understand that. Discretion is really important, and we teach that and we train that with our officers.

Senator ROBERTS: Is there an ongoing training program for AFP officers in relation to rapidly evolving legislation relevant to the issues I've raised today? Mr Nutt alluded to a number of pieces of legislation that have come in, in recent years.

We also work closely with the Attorney-General's Department, which has responsibility with respect to Commonwealth legislation, and it provides materials not only to us but also to our state and territory partners on guidance in the application of Commonwealth offences, particularly new ones.

I won't speak on behalf of the Attorney-General's Department, but when we have new legislation that relates to areas of mutual interest with our state and territory police we provide that advice to them by essentially circulating the Attorney-General's Department's material. Senator ROBERTS: This is my last question, Chair. There has been a lot of violence displayed on the internet and on TV—news et cetera—for the last 12 months or so. Mr Nutt : Perhaps where I'll take that question is that we've had some success with a relatively new offence relating to the possession and communication of violent extremist material. This offence focuses on material that portrays terrorist acts. It is also material that aids—in terms of education—in the carrying out of violent acts in the advancement of a religious, political or ideological cause.

Since this offence was introduced, it has been quite effective in the early identification of individuals who are consuming and potentially acting on violent extremist material. You may note that in the last week we had our first conviction under these provisions. We were very concerned about the violent extremist material that that individual had. We're concerned because of the nature of the material and how accessible it is—building on what the commissioner has already said, in terms of the role and responsibility of internet service providers and the like in preventing the spread, distribution and access to violent extremist materials—and more broadly around end-to-end encryption. When it comes to our young people and vulnerable people more generally, we have noted the digital algorithms that may come into play of people's internet activity and developed what has generally been considered to be echo chambers where someone looking up something may be pushed along or drawn along a path. The result being increased exposure to violent extremist material. We're quite concerned about that as an issue.

Senator ROBERTS: To build on your answer—and thank you for the answer—I'm guessing the AFP does a lot more intelligence work these days as a proportion of its overall crime fighting than it used to because of the internet.

CHAIR: Don delivers. Senator Polley has been waiting very patiently. There was a very important development today in an area of your concern, Senator Polley, so I'll hand the call to you.

Mr McCartney : Thank you, Senator, and thank you for your ongoing interest in this crime type. I spoke last time, and it does feel like only a couple of weeks ago. I think it was.

Senator POLLEY: It was.

Mr McCartney : The partnerships, particularly in this crime type, are absolutely crucial in terms of public, private and NGOs. In the work that we do in this space, we have over 250 different partners both domestically and across the world. One of our best partners is the eSafety Commissioner and the work that we've done and the work that we've continued to do over the last number of years. The MOU that was signed today is, in effect, the second MOU. We've signed a previous MOU. It highlights the foundations of the relationship we have with the eSafety Commissioner at the practical level.

I go to your question. What it is really focused on is enhancing the already close relationship we've got with the eSafety Commissioner to enable real-time intelligence and referral sharing in relation to online child exploitation. The AFP led ACCCE facilitates this through embedding eSafety personnel into our intelligence fusion cell, so it's very much a joint approach. We've collectively enhanced our processes for sharing information to ensure they're fit for purpose and efficient to increase the pace at which we can analyse the material and respond. That goes back to the question that Senator Shoebridge asked in terms of how we analyse this data and the ability, importantly, to identify emerging threats. So how do we stay ahead of the curve? It's an important document and a very important relationship, and we were very happy to sign that document today.

Senator POLLEY: Are there any new specific capabilities?

Mr McCartney : Yes. We need to change the volume of data that is coming in. One of challenges is the challenges we face through technology in terms of the volume of data, which Senator Shoebridge has referred to. There's the issue of encryption, which the commissioner has referred, and there's the issue of artificial intelligence.

In terms of the issue of partnerships, it would be remiss of me not to mention Operation Cumberland, which is an operation that has been coordinated out of Europol and led by the Danish police, but we've had very close cooperation in that. It's an international investigation into the production and sale of artificial intelligence generated child abuse material, which is particularly concerning. The commissioner has been on the record saying that AI produced material is getting so good that we just simply can't tell the difference. This operation was led by the Danish police, coordinated through Europol and involved law enforcement agencies from 19 countries, including Australia. Globally, 25 suspects were arrested and 33 premises searched. Operation Cumberland highlights the effect of international cooperation that we put in place in relation to this.

In terms of Australia, it resulted in the arrest of two individuals in Queensland and one in New South Wales being charged with offences in relation to possessing and using a carriage for child abuse material. Two of the three suspects had AI-generating software, which is particularly concerning. This is an example of great international cooperation, but I highlight the threat of artificial intelligence. I think that's an emerging threat. We've been on the record to say that we need to use technology to counter the threat that technology brings, but we need to be responsible in the use of that technology.

Senator POLLEY: Can you inform us as to the leading nations, in terms of anyone who is leading the way beside ourselves, in relation to AI child exploitation?

Mr McCartney : I think the commissioner would say that we are, but, again, it's very much a partnership approach. Senator POLLEY: With this memorandum of understanding, though, there are benefits beyond addressing child sexual exploitation. Can you outline to us capabilities in that area, where this memorandum, working with the commissioner, can be used.

Senator POLLEY: Can I move on quickly to the Pacific. You've come before us for a number of years now, and we've talked about the changes and how significant the relationships that we have are. Can you give us an update on what's happening?

Senator POLLEY: It would be helpful to have a better understanding of what the key priorities are in the ongoing partnership we have with those international partnerships.

Ms Gale : In the Pacific?

Senator POLLEY: In the Pacific.

Mr Kershaw : Part of it is our threat to democracy and making sure that we're supporting all those police forces in enforcing the rule of law and the principles of the rule of law and, in particular, helping those regional centres of excellence that the deputy's talked about. There'll be other training as far as being a detective, doing search warrants and a whole range of things. That centre is really critical to us. It's in a warm location too, not in Canberra. It's in Brisbane, which is important. There is a lot of activity that's going on.

We are also encouraging our New Zealand cousins to assist where they can. We're working hand in glove with the New Zealand commissioner around how we build capability and uplift in the region. As you're aware, our region is quite vulnerable our there. Even from my recent travel to Fiji, I was able to understand their needs at a deeper level of what they were looking for from Australia and the AFP. Ms Gale : Senator, I can just offer that, in addition to what the commissioner has said, there are actually three key pillars that underpin the initiative. One of them, which we will use the hub in Brisbane for, is the Pacific Police Support Group. That's approximately 40 officers from 11 countries across the Pacific, and that is like a multinational deployable pool that can be deployed where required. Ms Gale : That's an excellent question. Mr Kershaw : I can assist the deputy. We've got 104 in the region, which is a significant investment. That includes Timor-Leste as well. The majority of our resources are mainly in the Melanesian countries. That's where the main cadre of all of our people is.

Mr Kershaw : Yes. I think the deputy commissioner is probably going to assist me. Certainly, organised crime have taken advantage of the fact that it's a highly profitable market for organised crime. The Illicit Tobacco Taskforce are working with Border Force, of course, who have the lead, and we're also working with our state counterparts. You've seen what's happened in Victoria, New South Wales and other parts of the country. We're certainly seeing it as a serious crime in particular, and the fact is that we've been able to use our Criminal Assets Confiscation Taskforce and all of the powers that the AFP can bring to the fight to assist our state colleagues. We've also been able to successfully—and I think the Border Force have done some really great work on illicit vapes and other things coming into this country, and also shipments of that tobacco. Senator POLLEY: What has that $49 million that was recently invested enabled you to do?

What I mean by that is that you have to meet or prove the elements of the definition of a 'terrorist organisation', if they're not proscribed, and those are—I will say broadly, not technically—that the organisation is engaged in the planning and preparation for or the undertaking of or advocating for a terrorist act. So the response is the security posture of critical infrastructure, which includes security of your people, your places and your information and technology. That's guided by the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act and other actions that happen between the government and the private sector. Security is very much a shared responsibility, but critical infrastructure owners are responsible for their security. Having coherent security strategies is the best defence, armed by an intelligence awareness of the likely threats that you're facing. Incoherence in some ideologies is maybe not so much a concern. Obviously, it depends on how you find it, and for us the challenge is that we're seeing a broadening number of reasons where a small number of people think violence is the answer. The other trend that's occurring is that they go to violence with little or no warning and little or no planning. That's exceptionally hard for law enforcement and security services to deal with, but it is a factor in our environment.
