We haven't gotten to the point where we're trying to look at complex performance measures, but that will come with time. I was the CEO of the New South Wales ICAC from its 30th anniversary through to its 35th. They had more complex and sophisticated performance measures, but that was on the basis that they had a long history of understanding how long it took to do investigations—those sorts of issues.

Senator SCARR: When I reflect on those KPIs, given the previous experience I had with the previous commissioner, Ms Hinchcliffe, who I think did a wonderful job—I think I've put that on the record, but I'll do it again—what immediately strikes me is the corollary, if you like. Eighty per cent need to be triaged within 90 days—

Mr Reed : Assessed.

Senator SCARR: Assessed—sorry. They must be assessed within 90 days. How do you measure the 20 per cent that's left in terms of it being resolved within an appropriate period?

Mr Reed : It's always going to be an outlier—

Senator SCARR: Sometimes they may be the more difficult—

Mr Reed : Absolutely.

Senator SCARR: or the more challenging cases, but they could also be the more important ones.

Mr Reed : That's true, and what happens in these assessment processes is that the triage process is quite binary. Is it a Commonwealth official? Is there a corruption issue? And a lot of what comes through the door can be excluded at that point. When you move the roughly 10 per cent across to the next stage of assessment, you've got to do a lot more work, and this is where preliminary investigations come in. As I identified earlier, we've got 34 of those underway at this point, and they can take a reasonable period of time, because they can involve notices being served to obtain further information to try and define the corruption issue. When you move into that phase, you are talking about much larger periods of time. But on the numbers overall, or the expected performance result of assessment within 90 days, largely, those matters in triage drag down the length of the tier 2 assessments. But this is a business that has been operating for roughly 21 months, and we're still working through the timeframes around these sorts of matters. There will definitely be outliers, and those are the 20 per cent. If we become clearer about how we would measure that or what a KPI around that might be, we may end up having to set a time limit for an assessment process, and then you start being marked much more critically on your success or failure.

Senator SCARR: The other KPI—the 60 per cent measure—is within two years.

Mr Reed : That's because, when that was set, we'd been in operation for 12 months; the investigative process had only been underway for roughly nine months. Therefore, there was a sense that we needed to put something forward, and therefore we made it a finalisation target of 60 per cent within two years. Again, there will be outliers. That's the area where, as the organisation matures and as we finalise or complete investigations, we will get a much better understanding of how long it takes to do an investigation. At ICAC, it was quite often three years—in that sort of order—and we would know that.

Senator SCARR: Again—and these were public inquiries—when I was a member of the select committee looking at the legislation establishing NACC, we received evidence from people who'd been through anticorruption type investigations. Some people have been exonerated, and one of the issues raised was that having such a matter hanging over you for an extended period of time can be quite difficult.

Mr Reed : Yes.

Senator SCARR: How do you deal with that issue?

Mr Reed : The difficulty with corruption is that it's a difficult area to investigate. It's challenging because it's usually conducted in secret. This is out of the opening address:

… its hallmarks are confidential communications and inscrutable exercises of power. Often it involves complex pathways of deception and deceit. Finding, testing, challenging and unravelling these necessarily takes time.

Under none of the models used by other entities do we see that any of those decisions are ever made public, because, of course, what you're trying to do is investigate something that there's an attempt to hide. Individuals are not aware for all of that time that they are being investigated, because there can be a covert period which can take a reasonable period of time before you go overt. But, where it has become overt and individuals—persons of interest—are aware, there is a challenge in terms of the length of time that it can take to actually complete that investigation or bring it to finality.

I think that, because of the experiences of other commissions around Australia, we've ended up having to, at the very beginning, introduce witness welfare and witness liaison officers to address some of these issues—the stresses that some people face during the processes of an organisation like the commission. That only emerged in the last six months of when I was at ICAC, so it hadn't been in place for nearly 35 years of their operations, but the experience of both ICAC and IBAC in Victoria and others was that you have to try and address the issues that are surrounding witnesses that are being investigated by organisations like this once they know that they're being investigated. So witness liaison becomes quite an important tool in the toolkit. You don't try to make them go forever, but, by necessity and with the number of investigations we're undertaking, they will take time.

Senator SCARR: I did note in your statement that you'd recruited three witness liaison officers. I was initially quite surprised at the number. Is that in response to the demand from witnesses?

Mr Reed : It was actually our desire, when we were doing the private hearings that I referred to earlier. It wasn't just in relation to the private hearings, but it becomes more intense as a result of private hearings. There would be persons of interest that we would be investigating. When you undertake things like executing search warrants or bringing people in for statements, there's quite a lot of emotional stress attached to that and, of course, mental health issues that may have existed and might emerge in that process. The witness liaison officers have turned out to be very important. The challenge is holding onto people in those sorts of roles. We initially started with one permanent, and then we ended up bringing in another temporary person for 12 months and then, as a result of some health issues, we ended up having to bring in the third person to take over some of those duties. So you probably need at least two people for the number of matters that we're dealing with and the number of witnesses that potentially emerge out of those processes.

Senator SCARR: But there's a distinction between a witness liaison officer and a witness support service, presumably. How do you define the line—

Mr Reed : It's quite clear that we're not meant to be providing the actual psychological support to those individuals. What we've got to try and do is ascertain who's most at risk and what sort of service we could put them in contact with. We have a contractual arrangement with one service provider, and then we provide people the opportunity to access that service, and we pay for that access. Now, there are a lot of people in this area of corruption activity that don't have any interest at all in those sorts of services, but there are vulnerable people that you come across that do need it, and none of us want to see anybody suiciding or even experiencing suicide ideation.

Senator SCARR: No. It was an issue that was considered by the select committee. In relation to the activities of the inspector, which was also something we consider as a select committee, I'm interested to understand how, from your perspective, the inspector's discharging of the statutory role to conduct an audit type activity to ensure that NACC is acting in accordance with the law and best practice occurs in practice, in terms of that audit as opposed to the complaints being made.

Mr Reed : Most of it at the moment is coming through complaints. We actually initiated our own audit of our evaluation process to look at the nature of matters that had been triaged out and provided that to the inspector. I think that, over time, we will move further on from the complaint issue. That's been quite an active process, because people complain regularly about what we have done or not done in relation to their referral. Some of those go to the inspector, and some of those then come back to us from the inspector. Others she deals with—I think she has described that in her annual report—without referring them to us, but she's very active and very clear that she has the ability to hold us to account for how we've actually undertaken the complaints. So, as I said, I think the audit function will become more over time than it is at the moment.

Senator SCARR: What did your own internal audit of, to again use your phrase, 'matters triaged out' indicate?

Mr Reed : That meant these matters were not proceeding to the tier 2 assessment, which was a more detailed assessment.

Senator SCARR: Sorry: I should have been more particular in my question. What was the result of the audit?

Mr Reed : The result of the audit was that there were a small number of those triaged matters that we felt we could have dealt with in a better way, but we didn't find any matters where there had been—and this is from my memory—a wrong decision made. That was what I was particularly keen to understand, because the inspector has clearly pointed out to us where she believed that there were errors in our triage process, and we've had to address those and, as I said, it's active in that space.

Senator SCARR: I've got two more questions. The first is about the finalisation of matters that were transitioned from ACLEI to NACC. There was always a thought in my mind about how successfully those matters would be triaged from ACLEI across to NACC and whether or not there would be any impact on the investigation process by the transition from authority 1 to authority 2. Is there anything you can comment in that regard?

Mr Reed : I suppose I wasn't in ACLEI, but I think we're effectively dealing with what was quite a reasonable number of matters that were transitioned across—22 matters. At the moment, seven of the 22 are still active investigations.

Senator SCARR: What's the oldest of those matters—even in ballpark figures? Is there one that's been ongoing for, say, five years or four years?

Mr Reed : I'm happy enough to take that on notice, because some of the matters had a reasonable age when they were transitioned, and here we are 21 months later.

Senator SCARR: That's why I was curious to know. One of the matters I was interested to see measurement of after NACC had had some time of being in operation was the number of matters that were referred to NACC and found to be outside the jurisdiction of NACC. There was always a query as to whether or not you'd be inundated and everyone who had a complaint about anything would be making an application to you. What's the experience been over the last 21 years—21 months? You might be there in 21 years!

Mr Reed : It could well be! I won't be but others might be.

Senator SCARR: I won't be!

Mr Reed : What we've identified—and it's in the opening address—is that, in the first year of operations, we received a total of 3,190 referrals. In the nine months since 1 July 2024, we've received another 1,636 referrals. In that sense, the number has reduced from that first year's operation. I couldn't predict what the number would be at the end of this financial year. We've still got another quarter to go. Sorry, there's breaking news here—we might be able to answer that question that you asked about what the oldest of the transition matters was.

Mr Ratcliffe : The oldest matter that transitioned from the LEIC Act to the NACC Act is an operation which commenced on 1 September 2021, and it's currently pending finalisation. There have been two convictions achieved, and, basically, we're just writing up after the court process.

Senator SCARR: Excellent, that's good.

Mr Reed : Sorry, I lost the train there.

Senator SCARR: Since 1 July 2024, there have been a further 1,636 referrals. So there's been a step change from the first year. People are discovering the jurisdiction et cetera. A total of 1,257 were excluded at the triage stage. What are the reasons for that exclusion? Obviously, a key reason can be jurisdiction.

Mr Reed : Yes. It's often: Is it actually a Commonwealth official that they're talking about? Is there a viable corruption issue in there?

Senator SCARR: Why else would a matter be excluded at the triage stage?

Mr Reed : Often, it's just completely irrelevant to our jurisdiction. That's just the nature. To a degree, we're probably going to be a place of last resort. People who are angry about government may not go to the ombudsman or they might go to the ombudsman and also come to us. So that's the nature.

Senator SCARR: Alright.

CHAIR: Senator Shoebridge.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE:   Mr Reed, the compulsory retirement age for the Army Reserve is 65 years. I believe Commissioner Brereton is 67 years of age. To retain his commission, was he required to seek the consent, permission or concurrence of the Chief of the Defence Force.

Mr Reed : I'd have to take that on notice.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Is the retention of his commission as a major general subject to any ongoing concurrence, consent or permission from the Chief of the Defence Force?

CHAIR: Senator Shoebridge, you know that's not a question for the NACC; that's a question for Defence.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: No. This utterly relates to a potential conflict of interest between the commissioner—

CHAIR: No. The question isn't relevant to the NACC estimates.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Mr Reed, are you aware of whether or not the retention of his commission as a major general is the subject of any ongoing permission, consent or concurrence of the CDF?

Mr Reed : Not that I'm aware of, but I don't know that. I'd have to take it on notice.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: We know some of the costs to the NACC of the adverse finding by the inspector of how Commissioner Brereton dealt with the robodebt matter include the cost of engaging Mr Nettle. That was more than $205,000. Is that right?

Mr Reed : I think it was around that figure. Let me just quickly—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Alright. We got some answers earlier today which said that Mr Nettle has been paid $185,000 for his work.

Mr Reed : No—$206,800 gross.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: That's $206,800.

Mr Reed : Gross.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Did the $206,800 that was paid to Mr Nettle for his reconsideration come from the NACC budget?

Mr Reed : Of course, yes.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Have there been any other external payments made by the NACC because of the adverse finding by the inspector against Commissioner Brereton?

Mr Reed : The AGS supported Mr Nettle to keep it at arm's length from the commission—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Did they bill you?

Mr Reed : and their work in this part of the consideration was $22,594.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Alright. So $229,000 of external costs have been paid because of the adverse finding of the inspector? Is that a yes.

Mr Reed : Well, if $22,594 and $206,800 adds up to that number, then, yes.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Are there any other costs that have been paid?

Mr Reed : No.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Mr Nettle provided his report to the commissioner on 10 February 2025.

Mr Reed : That's correct.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: But there was no media release published until 18 February 2025.

Mr Reed : That's correct.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: What explains the delay?

Mr Reed : Mr Nettle sent his report quite late on 10 February to the commissioner. The commissioner then distributed it the following day to statutory officeholders and senior staff of the commission for consideration. We then, with me being the primary person managing what was going to happen next—because, as you'd be aware, Mr Nettle made the decision that we were investigating; we didn't have to make a decision following the report about whether we were going to investigate or not—part of the delegation to Mr Nettle was to decide whether or not to investigate. So, on that basis, it was then: what did we have to put in place and what advice were we going to need in terms of how we would then undertake that process so that we would be in a position to be able to at least identify what we would do as a result of the decision by Mr Nettle that we were going to investigate these six persons of interest that were referred to us by the royal commission. So there were a number of procedural things we needed to do. Based on our procedural fairness processes, we had to advise those six people of interest. We had done that at each step of the process up to that point when the decision was made—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: You say that was procedural fairness, Mr Reed, but you say in your answers to questions on notice it was a standard welfare procedure. Was it procedural fairness or a standard welfare procedure?

Mr Reed : The two things were intertwined when it came to the persons of interest. You're going to deliver news that was unexpected or potentially unexpected by these people, who had been told around 6 June 2024 that they were not going to be the subject of an investigation. They were then told that the inspector was doing an investigation into how we had handled the matter and that, as a result, there would be reconsiderations. So we advised them about that occurring. We had advised them about the fact that we were doing the reconsideration, and then we advised them about the outcome of the investigation. From our perspective, when you're dealing with any person of interest, you have to take witness welfare into account. It's not something that you do for one person and not for another. Now, it might be ignored by those individuals—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I was asking you about procedural fairness.

Mr Reed : When it comes to procedural fairness—we're doing a fact sheet, which will be put on our website probably tomorrow or Monday, which describes the procedural fairness provisions that we have—therefore, what we're doing is advising people about something that is going to occur. We are trying to make sure that they are—

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: This is advising them about a decision that's been made. How is there an obligation of procedural fairness to advise them about a decision that's been made?

Mr Reed : We believe that it's important that we advise people about what's coming up and what's coming next—not them reading about it in the media.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: This is my final question. I put an FOI in to request, amongst other things, the draft and any alterations to the media release that was issued.

Mr Reed : Yes, that's correct.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: We now know that the commissioner made suggestions and amendments to the media release.

Mr Reed : That's correct.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: And you have refused to produce any drafts or any communications in relation to the media release, alleging that the media release contains deliberative material and extends beyond factual material and that drafting the media release included the crafting of an opinion and an evaluation of information. Is that really your view—that draft media releases—

Mr Reed : I'm not the decision-maker when it comes to FOI.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: let me finish—that draft media releases are excluded from the FOI because they are—

Mr Reed : I'm not the decision-maker when it comes to FOI. We've dealt with, I think, a hundred to date, and it's a very active process within the organisation.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I'll make it simple. Will you provide to this committee the draft media release, any communications with the commissioner and any alterations the commissioner made to the media release?

Mr Reed : Well, we didn't provide it in the FOI. I'll take it on notice.
